items.title: Austin trip day three: Robotaxi day. Coffee, tacos, and haircuts paid in sats.
items.text:
Hey stackers,

Writing from the hotel after another action packed day here in Austin. I haven’t played poker yet today so here is a Hand breakdown of one I played around midnight last night after making my day two post.

https://stacker.news/items/1603804/r/SatAttack?commentId=1604264

Woke up rather late again but I was fine with that today as I didn’t really have any set plans. Other than exploring and slanging sats I had one goal for today—ride a Robotaxi! They have their own  app which I had installed yesterday and got my account all set up and quickly ordered my ride. You get two choices. A two seater that doesn’t have a steering wheel and has a ton of leg room or a four seater that does have a steering wheel and less leg room (but still plenty). The two seater is always slightly more expensive but I wanted to try that first so that’s what I ordered. It only took five minutes for it to show up to my hotel.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163752)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163753)

Pretty slick looking I thought. But the most impressive part about it by far is the way it drives. It was very cool and I really enjoyed cruising around in this thing. Gave a lot of time to contemplate how this might shape and evolve the future of cities. And I’m torn honestly. On one hand roads and parking take up so much city space and resources to accommodate the car and proliferates infrastructure that makes owning a car mandatory. I love a city built for the walkers and bikers. On the other hand I can’t see this business model doing anything but expanding rapidly. It just worked so so well. The price was competitive to other ride share options, the product worked incredibly, and being alone in there without social friction was really refreshing. It  was really enjoyable to look around the city while some…thing else drove me to my destination.

Which was another Medici Roasters! I needed to start my day with another red eye. As we (the car and I) got closer to our destination I was more and more pleased with my decision to not drive myself. I didn’t know when I  booked but this coffee shop is located directly across the street from University of Texas, Austin. It’s on Guadalupe St. right in in the middle of a big college town. Tons of traffic, people, and shops. No parking. Perfect job for Robotaxi.

This Medici is HUGE. Much much bigger than the previous one and it’s full of students on lap tops and reading books and such. At the counter I ordered my red eye and again I didn’t need to bother asking if I could pay in bitcoin. They had the square terminal with the toggle option. They also had a sign that said “pay with bitcoin” so that’s great. I contemplated asking the cashier lady about people paying with bitcoin but it was so busy and bustling I didn’t want to waste her time. So I silently paid with Phoenix and shortly after walked upstairs with my coffee.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163754)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163755)

I chilled and read and sipped my coffee before heading out on foot to cruise the city I was dropped off in. I didn’t really have an agenda. Quickly though I ended up in a second hand store called 2nd street. They had some nice looking clothes in there and I still needed a dressy undershirt for  a wedding tomorrow. No bitcoin accepted sign there unfortunately but I got a nice shirt for $9.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163756)

Onward into the college town. Nearly every person and building has some Texas Longhorn attire on it. There were frat and sorority houses, all sorts of food and clothing shops, and orange bull heads every where I looked.
Everyone seemed to be anticipating a game between Texas and Mississippi state. I probably should have taken a picture but one fraternity house had a huge sign in the front of it with a football player urinating on what I assume was the Mississippi state mascot. “Go Long Horns. Piss on miss” it said. I walked where ever my mind decided was the direction to go for about an hour before deciding it was time to eat. There was an overwhelming amount of options but one taco stand caught my eye. Closed unfortunately. But that at least set my mind on what I wanted.

So I cruised around sure I would happen upon another source of tacos and lo and behold, I was gifted a spot. It’s called Don Vegas tacos. Tucked away with some other food trucks and brick and mortar food places with benches and ample seating. I notice they have a square terminal and start to get hopeful… could it be?

I took the opportunity to practice my Spanish and ordered five street tacos and a jamaica agua fresca. When she rung me up sure enough the toggle to Bitcoin option was available!! “Yo pago con bitcoin!” I said. Which is a bit broken, but she understood. And she was excited! No one had ever done it before she said. I didn’t talk about bitcoin too much but just explained how some square terminals allow it and some don’t. Another successful lightning transaction, I knew, would make my tacos taste much better. They didn’t need the help though… they were soooo good. Con tortillas hechas a mano  they were so fresh and warm and perfect. I got carne asada. They came with limes and fried onions and cheese and avocado and cilantro. Heavenly. Mi jamaica complimented them very well too. This was a great experience because I was just looking for tacos, not a place to spend bitcoin. But I found both out in the wild.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163760)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163761)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163762)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163763)

I forgot to mention. Earlier in my Robotaxi the screen kept giving me recommendations on different commands to give or ask Grok. “Make the car feel like a sling morning in Kyoto” “what would happen if the moon disappeared” but I decided on my own prompt. “Hey Grok,” “can you give me places where I can spend bitcoin for a haircut?” And it gave me several. It said it referenced bitcoincities.org which I had never heard of. Seems to be some similar  project to BTCmap. Grok gave me three options:

Royalties Barber

Geiser barber

South Austin barber

After finishing mis tacos y jamaica I started to go down the list with phone calls to ask if they do in-fact  accept bitcoin. First call Royalty’s didn’t pick up at all. So I called Geiser. Someone quickly answered and I said I’ve got kind of a weird question… will you accept bitcoin there? “Oh sure I accept bitcoin…” a bit hesitantly. He said it had been a while and only one other person (a repeat customer) had done it. I asked if he used square and he said yes. “That should take care of us” I assured. It was 1 pm and we settled on an appointment time of 330 PM.

So I had a couple hours to kill and decided to go do something I’ve wanted to do since my walk with @Scoresby on day one: rent a paddle board and cruise the river! So I booked my second Robotaxi. I chose the cheaper four door option this time. Again the car was quick to show up and I had another pleasant and impressive drive to my destination. Lady bird lake rentals.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163764)

This little box didn’t accept bitcoin or cash so I had to use a credit card but they quickly had me on my way to the dock on the river. I had to hike a tiny bit but it was pretty out so all good. I’ll let these pictures describe the experience:

![](https://m.stacker.news/163765)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163766)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163767)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163768)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163769)

That bridge is the same bridge @Scoresby showed me that first day where all the bats live. I used it as my turn around point and could hear those bats again. I dropped off my paddle board at about 240 and ordered my third Robotaxi of the day for destination haircut.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163770)

Geiser Barbering was on this quiet street in a cute little commercial building that look to once be a house. Very pleasant experience here. Nick is a master barber and beardsman. He has one single high quality barbers chair and I ordered a straight razor clean shave and a basic haircut in preparation for the wedding tomorrow. We talked a lot the whole time. He was interested in my traveling and poker playing. He has a life long friend who is a full-time poker pro so we related on that topic a lot. Earlier I had seen a “get Elon’s dirty money out of Austin!!” Sign plastered multiple times on the side of a building and was curious what his opinion of the Robotaxi was. He had only done it once as a joy ride with his wife but was equally as impressed as I was.

We talked about bitcoin in Austin and his experience with it. He said he loves accepting bitcoin because it’s free to do so and that he knows a lot of self-identified bitcoiners but none of them like to spend it. He said mainly it’s because they’re afraid of tax obligations. I told him all my favorite parts about bitcoin and I was glad he was willing to accept. He was glad I was willing to pay. He would be using square to auto invert to USD however. We talked a lot about Bitcoin and merchants and what may or may not happened in the future. He said he’d  love it if more people started to spend so that “us merchants” can start to learn and use it more too. He was a cool chatty guy and very willing to have a nice conversation about it.

The straight razor shave was great. He had me all lathered and lotioned and hot toweled and he apparently doesn’t use an alcohol based after shave. It’s for the birds he said. Instead he uses an antiseptic chalk base after shave that feels and works better to seal everything up. I agreed, it was comforting. All spick and span it was time to settle. He uses square on his phone and pretty quickly used it to present a lightning invoice which I paid with no issues. I tipped in cash, saving some sats.

He had mentioned that he some times goes to Medici and I thought it would be cool to ask if I could tip him further with bitcoin and try to get him to spend it on a coffee but I didn’t follow through. The service was a bit pricey already and I was scared to recommend some wallet that I wasn’t familiar with that would be easy for him to use.

I ordered my fourth and final Robotaxi of the day that would conclude today’s adventure and bring me back to my hotel. The ride was a projected traffic-filled thirty minutes but I didn’t mind at all because I knew I would just be chillin and gazing out the window. “RelaxiTaxi!” (IYKYK)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163773)

Instead of window gazing though I asked Grok to pull up my favorite chess grandmaster Eric Hanson. His videos relax me and his chess is wonderful to watch. I’ve been a big fan of the Chessbrahs for many years.

Another great action packed day here in Austin and I’ll be heading out for a few hours of poker very soon.

If you missed day one and two you can check them out here.

Day one: https://stacker.news/items/1602995

Day two: https://stacker.news/items/1603699

Thanks for reading and following along!

items.title: Trunk or Treat 2026 - This post has free free ecash.
items.text:
# 2024 - snickerbar.me

For Halloween of 2024, I had been experimenting with ecash and was having a blast with stacker.news. I decided to pass out ecash tokens to the parents of trick or treaters to encourage bitcoin adoption in our neighborhood. I forked cashu.me and engaged in some coding that was way over my head and mostly a learning experience for me. The results varied from "eh" to "aight" and fun was had by all. I chronicled that spooky season in [a post exposing my coding ineptitude](https://stacker.news/items/717596), [making a spooky crossword puzzle for stackers](https://stacker.news/items/723313), [iterating](https://stacker.news/items/729712), [mashing up Janet Yellen and Metallica to @DarthCoin's delight](https://stacker.news/items/748546), and ultimately [passing out small amount of sats while playing music by David Lynch on a DX-7](https://stacker.news/items/748618).

![](https://m.stacker.news/56707)

![](https://m.stacker.news/60570)

It was a fun time.

# 2025 - They don't celebrate Halloween in Mossel Bay

South African townships have witches. I never met one, but I heard quite a bit about them, and sadly, it was mostly from scared children. I've been told that the witches are responsible for gangs, substance abuse, and general violence in the townships. What was very sad to me was the amount of talismans I saw children wearing to "protect" themselves from witches. There is a very real bondage there, and as I was in Mossel Bay for Halloween 2025, we kept it low key and at home.

My wife and I personally do believe that there is a supernatural realm, but are thoroughly convinced that talismans, incantations, and other charms do nothing to protect people from evil. So, at home, we kept our American traditions, which are solely for fun and pretend. We made costumes out of paper. The kids did trick or treat to the rooms my wife and I separated to in the two bedroom apartment. We used what was available to make little jack 'o lanterns.

And in doing so, almost burnt the place down.

If you're wondering, no, I do not recommend at this point that you fill a gem squash with kerosene soaked fire starters.

We finished the night with some kid-friendly spooky stories. Alas, last Halloween featured no caramel apples, no hayrides, no corn mazes, and worst of all, NO ECASH!

items.title: Freshman Dem Members & Supporters Are Quickly Finding Out The Hill Is Different
items.text:
Earlier today, a colleague brought to my attention that people are rapidly finding out that The Hill does not operate in what I would call a normal way, and that being in the Majority is flat-out hard. Freshman Members arrived in DC over the weekend (and are actually staying at a hotel that is by my apartment.... security is insane) for the 120th Congress Freshman Orientation held in the Capitol.

With the Freshman Members making their first trek to DC since the election is has brought with it a ton of individuals wanting to make a statement. There have been a few rallies and protests in the district that backed this up but yesterday was the first time I saw/an alert was sent out to avoid an area because of these groups. 

Ironically, these people had no idea where they should be because it was aimed at the Expected to Be Speaker Jefferies; however, they had it in a Senate Building. The goal of the groups that were there was to get the Future Speaker to prioritize what they wanted. One group was for reproductive rights, another was for the environment, and I want to say there was a third, but I can't remember what their priority was. Now, these were clearly Democratic supporters; however, the Capitol Police soon had to start arresting them... because they started to fight each other over who was correct in what should be the priority..... I kid you not.... Grown adults who support the same person.... fighting each other because they want their thing to be the priority.... all while they are on the completely wrong side of Congress.... Just incredible. 

Thinking back, that should have probably been a sign to me of the things that were to come. Yesterday was also the first day I saw on TV various Senators, in particular, speaking out against Sen. Chuck Schumer becoming the Senate Leader. Which absolutely blows my mind. If you factor in the two outstanding races flipping Dem, you end up with a 9-seat flip. This would be the largest flip since President Eisenhower was in office in 1958. It would be the largest since the U.S. was 50 states. 


The idea to then take the person who was in charge of Senate Dems and, in a lot of ways, punish him by not giving him the promotion that comes with leading your party to victory would frankly be insane. For better or worse, Schumer has been Leader of the Senate when he had to deal with Trump being the President, and to put someone else in that role frankly seems like a backhanded move. During a time when the elections resulted not only in a party flip but also in many who won in Republican areas being much more middle-of-the-road, installing a leftist favorite in Van Hollen doesn't exactly make the most sense. Likely future Speaker Jeffries is facing the exact same issue when he was able to reverse Republican/Trump 2024 inroads with various groups and make the Democratic Party have a much larger tent. 

Nowhere is the absolute meltdown of the far left and leftists more evident than on the Instagram account "Dear_White_Staffers." This account is well known on The Hill by both sides due to the far-left propaganda they post. Over the last few years, since I have followed them, they have really ended up losing the plot on a lot of things, and when the American people would vote, and it turns out things like open borders were not popular, the account would kinda melt down. Now the same thing is happening once again because Democratic Leader Jeffries sent out an email reminding the freshmen that the funding that he and his leadership team have done got them into office, and it was under his leadership that, frankly, the Party was able to accomplish such a landslide just a week and a half ago. 

Apparently, these Freshmen and their supporters thought that they could take the money, networks, endorsements, etc. that Leader Jefferies gave them and not pay the piper. While it does seem that most of the Freshman House Members understand this, their supporters are losing their collective minds. 

Across both the House and the Senate, particularly in the Democratic Party due to their party rules, traditions, etc., seniority is a huge, huge thing. To be honest, it makes sense as well. I mean, it is often the case that new members do not have the connections or understanding of why some things are the way that they are, and the catastrophic issue that would occur is that various laws and statutes would suddenly and dramatically change. So many of the people on both sides miss this critical issue, and when they run into it rather than tell anyone why they changed, they just pivot or blame the system. The system can be changed; it just isn't a quick fix, and Members on both sides and in both chambers want quick and easy wins. 

There is a post on Dear_White_Staffers that is from someone named _meganthuy that highlights how narrow-minded these leftists are. In her post, she came out bashing the Moderates of her party (those that you know represent the red states and red areas that Democrats won it) because those individuals, multi-term winners and freshmen included, do not want the party to go overboard and immediately make moves to abolish ICE, cut all funding to Israel, outright ban frontier AI and data centers, etc. She said that these issues are the reason that the moderates won, ignoring the clear data that showed that, frankly, prices are too damn high and Republicans have failed to lower them plus got them into another war. 

This 20-something thinks that you can enact far-left legislation while failing to do the math, just like Republicans did with the SAVE Act. If you can deal with fragmenting your party in the House, you still need 60 Senate seats, and frankly, Dems don't have it. That's before we even get to the whole the President is Donald Trump issue, who has said he has no issue vetoing things. 

This girl further goes on to say that there were a lot of people who reluctantly voted Democratic and that they did so only to stop the war, but immediately follows it up with these much further-left ideas, like abolishing ICE instead of reforming it. Throughout the video, she highlights how they won because of XYZ but then follows it up by ignoring those things and focusing on things that do not address XYZ that got those Democratic Members elected. 

I thought with a margin of victory as large as the House and Senate were that the internal division issues that both leaders would face would fall by the wayside, but apparently... that's not the case. As a result, I see two possible outcomes, and that is either common sense wins out, and the far left goals will be reigned in or the far left is going to blow their legs off by nuking the best-suited person to deal with the wide array of groups representing the party and nuking the idea of passing anything for the next two years. Whoever is the leader of the House and Senate is going to have to be people who want to get a deal done, plain and simple. Trump is known as someone who loves a deal, and if you remove the dealmakers and place combative people who clearly are not going to cut a deal, like these outspoken internet people and people currently on The Hill, your end result is going to be two wasted years, with the Republican Party able to identify and leverage unpopular issues against Dems two years from now.

items.title: Burning Electricity for Yet More Sats: 21 Energy and their new Ofen 3 Pro
items.text:
*Alternative title:* “3,000 sats a day keeps the doctor away.” *We’re all heatpunks now*!

I hinted at this *a little* already... (https://stacker.news/items/1611882?commentId=1612301, https://stacker.news/items/1613701?commentId=1613729, https://stacker.news/items/1530104)... and finally, today is the day: 

**3,000 words on what it's like to earn 3,000 sats a day.**

In April I posted “[Burning Electricity for 115,000 sats](https://stacker.news/items/1466211)” recapping the experience of having run the Ofen 2 for a few months during winter. For this season, the 21 Energy team graciously sent me their [newest machine](https://21energy.com/products/ofen-3?variant=60451037610318) for review: the **Ofen 3 Pro**.

([Black Week party](https://21energy.com/collections/sales) over there for the next two weeks with *nice juicy prices* if you’re in the market for a home miner! Rivaling [America’s Heatbit](https://bitcoinmagazine.com/business/heat-your-home-while-earning-bitcoin-with-heatbit "https://bitcoinmagazine.com/business/heat-your-home-while-earning-bitcoin-with-heatbit") and the [recent launch](https://www.youtube.com/post/UgkxrtV48gyqN4mygV9xisDudvb_f1b-BrE5 "https://www.youtube.com/post/UgkxrtV48gyqN4mygV9xisDudvb_f1b-BrE5") of its water heater, 21 Energy also just launched a full central heating system called [Focavo](https://21energy.com/de/pages/central-heating). Looks impressive!)

Largely boosted by the recent -9% difficulty adjustment — another metric that normal Bitcoiners don’t care much for but makes miners’ and heatpunks’ eyes go *ka-ching!* — I [breached 3,000 sats](https://x.com/joakimbook/status/2122652928636825847) on a (daily) payout for the first time. That was cool and unexpected.

**Agenda**:

* *User Experience*: what it’s like to use the Ofen 3 Pro (including pics and comparisons to Ofen 2)
* *Raw Numbers:* with all the juicy deets — speaking db, kWh, hashprice, J/TH etc etc
* *The Economic Case for Home Miners*: Returns, and Diminishing Returns
* *Financialization* of Now vs Later

***

## The Glorious User Experience: PICS OR DIDN'T HAPPEN!

This is what we're talking about:

![](https://m.stacker.news/168156)

It's **a machine that eats electricity and spits out heat and sats.** *Simple as that.*

I’ve always found these machines astonishingly beautiful. (Even the Ofen 1, which was a coffee-table type stand, *made me drool in envy!*)
Nothing like the sad, ugly, dusty, worn-out, and plastic-covered electrical heaters that I’m used to in my house.

When you set up the Ofen (both 2 and 3) and it starts hashing, it’s like the fans, firmware, and the ASICs inside need to learn *how* to run at each level. It takes a few days and a few tries for the machine to “get it” at every level. I remember this from my first product, thinking it was broken: *Every time* I would change the settings (from Two to Three, or Three to Four, or Four to One), it would restart itself.

...And if you’ve ever toyed around with any sort of miner, restarting means *loud, crazy fan noises* for an unpredictable while. (Chips gotta cool; machinery gotta clear; the ghost in the machines do their thing.) More than once has this sort of restarting — even after an unannounced firmware too early in the morning — woken me up to incessant fan noises in the next room.

*Oh. This is a good moment to explain how the app that controls the machines works.*

It’s a sleek, green-themed app with five levels that I’ll just call **One**, **Two**, **Three**, **Four** — and **Rocket**. It’s pretty simple, very beautiful, and the machines come with a thermostat that records ambient temperature inside. I don’t really use the thermostat function much (that automatically increases or decreases the hashing to keep a specific temperature) but prefer to manually adjust whenever I feel like they’re too loud for the occasion; I’m outside or it’s cold; or the hashprice is good etc etc.

The inside temperature of my house depends quite a lot on the outdoor weather condition (wind, surprisingly, is more important than temperature) so I just turn the machines up/down whenever it’s appropriate.

![](https://m.stacker.news/168155)

![](https://m.stacker.news/168163)

App interface is very simple, and my only complaint has been a handful of times when turning the Ofen 2 on and off, the app has “frozen” in off mode for days at a time. No way to *manually* or *physically* turn the machine on: there's no "On" button. (To turn it *off*, I can just asymmetrically pull the cord…)

I’ll highlight some of the differences here between the upgraded Ofen 3 Pro and the previous generation, even though the Ofen 2 (or that desirable table stand) is no longer for sale... in case someone is considering whether the upgrade is worth it, etc:

1. **The weight**. It’s significantly lighter, to the point where it (almost) feels like the Ofen 3 seems less sturdy than the original one. Delicate even. The company reps told me about a *third* less heavy (17 kg vs 25 kg for the prev one).
2. **The fan setup**. From the back, the air intake is completely different: two visible fans instead of the larger grid-type filter on the back of the Ofen 2.
3. **Fewer screws**. Way fewer (compare the back side of the machines in the images). Quite possibly why the metal (aluminium?) feels like it's holding itself together less.
4. **Sound:** feels slightly different — lighter or higher-pitched, somehow — and measuring them running on the same level, e.g., Two, they both register 42 dB a feet in front of them but the old one shows 36 dB from the middle of the room, whereas the Ofen 3 Pro shows 32 dB from a distance. (Might depend on the echoes of the room: I didn’t swap the Ofens to double-check; more on noise below.)

![](https://m.stacker.news/168157)

![](https://m.stacker.news/168158)

![](https://m.stacker.news/168159)

![](https://m.stacker.news/168160)

![](https://m.stacker.news/168161)

![](https://m.stacker.news/168162)

***Running Bitcoin miners:***

It’ll take you longer to fiddle with the pool settings than to get the stand screwed on and the electric cord plugged in. **Actually, your biggest trouble is deciding *where* in the house to place the miner.** I was a little concerned about where I might blow a fuse at the highest levels, and also wondered about the fan noise propagating through the house at various times of day.

21 Energy headlines the Ofen 3 for *top* hashing at 60 TH/s, drawing 1100 W.  I learned from the first machine that nobody but a pure psychopath wants to run them at peak effect for longer than a one-time experiment. *Too loud, too inefficient.*

Turning on the Rocket level this morning (just to try and to do my duties and provide the stackers with some raw numbers), the fan spun up markedly from the already loud Four. My measuring device said **it pulled *at the very most* 1278 W… *scheisse* ... but then settled down on a regular 1180W or so.** At first, it pulled that *while* cycling lower into the 40s and 30s TH/s, before going higher — standard miner behavior when switching pace.

I expected the efficiency to trail off markedly, as it does/did with my Ofen 2 at higher settings, but for the Ofen 3 Pro it stayed fairly intact: at *max* effect, which I clocked at **63.7 TH/s** (only caught the screenshot a moment after that one upwick), it remained at around 19 J/TH, astonishingly enough.

Also, that is a pretty good example of how *switching* between the levels is costly (“slippage”) in the efficiency department… it takes a while (sometimes upward of half-an-hour) for the miner to get to its optimal hashing level.

Glad to know my fuses can take that, in case it gets *really cold and stormy* and I want to squeeze out every last drop of hashing heat. The noise from the highest setting was orders of magnitude worse: 47dB in the middle of the room (57dB right in front of the miner), which is a pretty good indicator of how rarely I will use this elevated setting: *never*.

Speaking less numerically about the sound level, on One and Two it’s barely noticeable: **the low murmur of the fans drowns into the background noise**. I live in an exceedingly quiet place, so I imagine anyone in a city, with ambient noise or people and neighbors or birds chirping, will barely even notice this. I keep the Ofen 3 Pro in the living room, separated from my bedroom by a thin door (and somewhat sturdier wall); unless there’s a storm outside, I won’t run it higher than Two or Three at night.
(I would *never* have one of these machines in my bedroom: I’m extremely sensitive to nighttime sounds and selective about what goes there.)

**On Three, the Ofen 3 Pro gives out about 44 TH/s (\~830 W), and it strikes a reasonable trade-off between background noise and heat, comfortably heating a large living room to above 70°F at outdoor temperatures of around freezing.**

…and I learned exactly how much of a difference this makes just the other day, when the outdoor temperature overnight went from freezing, or low-30s, to 42°F... I woke up that morning to the living room and the office both at a boiling 77°F. *Dont need that much heat!*

As I’m writing this, I’m in shorts and t-shirt in the office (24.1°C, 75°F) with nothing but the Ofen 2 in here, running Two and giving off \~24 TH/s. (When I took the screenshot above, I had turned it off... too warm.) In the living room, where the Ofen 3 sits, the app says 22.8°C (73°F) and I’ve had it on Two for 32 TH/s for most of the afternoon.

## The Raw Numbers

Everybody knows that you can’t rely on a company’s headline, on-paper numbers. Not that they intentionally *lie* (one hopes...), but that they might have run the machines in ideal conditions and taken the best numbers, rather than the average or typical uses in the wild.

Similarly, I can’t know if my specific chips are good, bad, extreme, or average compared to other Ofen 2/3 products: **All I can do is report what *these ones* give off.**

For most of this year when I’ve been running the Ofen 2 (on Two or Three mostly) and measuring it, its efficiency has hit *about* 21 J/TH, sometimes, during long stretches, it’s reliably come down to the lower 20s: 20.2, 20.5. At the **18-19.5** that I’m getting with the new Ofen 3 Pro, it’s *nowhere near the 25% better efficiency* the company advertises... but still a decent improvement overall (7%-15%).

All-time payouts from the pool amount to over **400,000 sats**, which feels pretty awesome. (I also have a tiny [Braiins Mini Miner](https://x.com/joakimbook/status/2123404937988334076), running around the clock at \~40W and giving me the lordly hashrate of 1 TH/s; I’ve had this since well before the 21 Energy products, so it skews the total pool numbers a bit.) Depending on difficulty adjustments/how much other hashrate there’s on the network, I’ve been regularly getting daily payouts of about **1,300 sats.**

The Ofen 2 for its first year, had an uptime of probably 90%: I only ever turned it off on extremely warm and sunny spring/summer days, with the sun basking my living room and office and turning it into a tomato-growing Icelandic greenhouse. That’s the *main* [advantage I have](https://youtu.be/2-txiZKNIRk?si=w0Kiri18AxJmTSF9&t=180) as a home miner: Compared to most other (home) miners, **I can usefully run my machines for more hours out of the day, for more days out of the year.**

Since the Ofen 3 Pro arrived about two weeks ago, I’ve run it nonstop. (Fair enough, we’ve had [snowy winter](https://primal.net/e/nevent1qqs8596gxdn9qv8fr6am9zt902jkmff89ajlvy9szc27gkcuf6c9t5s6hee9l) with freezing temperatures this entire time.) Boosted by the [recent hashrate downturn](https://x.com/joakimbook/status/2122652928636825847), I’ve routinely had payouts of 2,700-3,000 sats… *that’s a neat little set-and-forget DCA.*

With *all* taxes and distribution fees included, my per-kWh expense comes out to about $0.17, most of which is tribute to the governmental mafiosos that run this place. (It would be about $0.15 at the more “normal” dollar FX rates we had before “Liberation Day.”) That’s not exactly cheap: Many [places in America](https://www.electricchoice.com/electricity-prices-by-state/) can bag better deals than that, but it’s not awful either. And much better than most places in Scandinavia, *tons* better than mainland Europe — something like half or one-third of residential electricity in Austria or Germany, two places having *tons of fun, staying electricity-poor.*

With today’s hashprice of [$0.03/TH/day](https://data.hashrateindex.com/bitcoin-compute-data/bitcoin-hashprice-index), and assuming I shove something like 65 TH/s/day on average onto the network from my three machines, my revenue comes out to little less than $2 a day. The electricity necessary to deliver 65 TH from these three machines come to about 1350 W (remember, at least *one* of those terahashes are from the very inefficient, but small, Braiins Mini Miner). Extrapolating out that usage, my heating *from these machines* — I, unfortunately, have a large one in the bedroom that I run sparsely at night and another in the bathroom — **costs me $5.62 a day for a daily loss of around $3.60.**

…but that’s *completely* the wrong way of thinking about mining bitcoin at home.

***

## Returns Everywhere: *Diminishing* Returns!

If you think miner profitability for two seconds, you realize that profitable mining *at residential rates* couldn’t possibly have made sense in the first place. As I wrote in the Nordic Node this summer (https://stacker.news/items/1530104)

> If a top-of-the-line machine from a few miner generations ago, optimized for use in the home (i.e., durable and *quiiiieeet*) were profitable on residential power rates, *you’d just scrap the guardrails and run it commercially for profit*.

Remember Tyler Stevens and Dylan Seib from [Exergy](https://www.exergyheat.com/) in their “[Bitcoin Home Mining Playbook](https://www.tftc.io/bitcoin-home-mining-playbook-exergy)” booklet, released together with TFTC: **your mining operation just has to be** [**useful**](https://fountain.fm/episode/BuLYdGnAhY8JjhSNe6Bw?t=344)**.** (https://stacker.news/items/1426924, https://stacker.news/items/1542390)

**> “You’re already paying for electricity to make heat. A miner converts the same electricity to the same heat and earns Bitcoin while it does. The electricity cost is identical.”**

The first heater I got — purchased with declining and ever-more worthless sats roughly at the peak of the 2025 euphoria — straight out replaced my 1500W electrical space heater. I wasn’t running that one on maximum around the clock (especially not on sunny spring and summer days), and unfortunately never kept good track of its usage. If I were to guess, I’d say something like 900W at 16 hours a day in winter, maybe 500W at 6 hours a day on average across summer months.

The price _insensitivity_ of this is what makes the home miners so competitive (well, "competitive") vs industrial corporate, AI-exposed miners. I don't *have* to pass a profit-and-loss test... I just have to be useful. And the waste heat (a problem for most industrial activities) is a benefit for me, *indeed the main point!*

That adds up to about **3,500 kWh in a typical year**. Add in the other electrical heaters in my house, and we’d probs be looking at some 5,000 kWh for annual heating purposes. (This estimate is probably lowballing *things quite a lot* because for the [three months I measured back in the spring](https://stacker.news/items/1466211), the *total household usage* was about 4,000 kWh; OK fine, light, coffee, fridge and the literal oven might account for quite a bit of that.)

Running the Ofen 2 at a weighted average of 494W (minus vacations/time away from house, downtime on extremely sunny and warm summer days etc.), and I’m probably looking at north of 4,000 kWh in a year for this machine alone.

With this *second* Ofen entering my home, the new one taking on the heavy heating duties of the old one, the first one is relegated to less important tasks. *Diminishing returns; Austrian econ and ordinal utility,* [*Böhm-Bawerk’s horses*](https://mises.org/mises-wire/why-austrians-stress-ordinal-utility) *etc*.
Meaning: The *Ofen 2* won’t burn 4,000 kWh this year... though its faster, nimbler sibling might: extrapolating its current 659W use (on Two) *for the entire year* gives me 5,772 kWh.

It’s not quite the dead of winter yet, and I’ve already permanently retired the two other small wall-attached heaters I used (500W and 400W respectively) — though never run at full blast, except for during the worst storms and cold, dark winter days. Also, the Ofen 2 now permanently sits in the office, and I’ve already turned it off a few hours a day on hot days (Including today). Presumably, its wonderful 90%+ uptime is gonna fall off *markedly* going forward… judging from the last two weeks, and adjusting for winter-summer, **all-year usage uptime might be about 50%**.
(Once I get my distribution company to install a smart meter https://stacker.news/items/1601880 and I bag a third off my rate during night hours, I might even *increase* my use a bit...)

**First**, then, I should consider the higher efficiency of the new machine. The *bulk* of my house’s heating will now happen at ^18 J/TH instead of ^20.5, routinely generating 30-40-50 TH/s instead of 20-30 TH/s as before. Probably not a kWh savings, but definitely a *sats* boost.

**Second**, with the other low-use heaters gone, the Ofen 2 is now displacing about 2,000 kWh a year… incidentally, what my previous use *times* 50% uptime would consume, meaning the \~1,300 sats a day attributable to *it* is a pure Pareto optimal improvement.

**Third**, quality-of-life adjustments. I definitely kept rooms I wasn’t using (e.g., the office during night) unheated before. Now I just let the Ofen 2 keep it warm all the time… *incredibly* nice to walk into the office in the morning and *not* be chilly. And, honestly, the same probably goes for the living room (where the Ofen 3 lives), and I’m keeping the ambient temperature higher than before.

**I don’t have a good final-figure/TL;DR conclusion here.** Going off vibes and feelz from the last two weeks: when I got the Ofen 2 last year, it *definitely reduced the total electricity use* compared to what I had been using. With the Ofen 3 Pro routinely using quite a bit more (800-900 W on higher levels or 650 on Two, versus Ofen 2’s 500-700W on those same levels), and the Ofen 2 displacing less than it will (probably) consume, I might actually start using *more* kilowatt-hours rather than fewer.

More heat, more sats, more fiat bills.

The upside of that is a) more sats, and b) better quality of life since I foresee keeping my home at a warmer temperature than I did before … and c) *looks better*! ( d) *I feel like a cool heatpunk...?)*

## The Sats Carry Trade: Financialization Mania

It’s the 21st century, and we live under fiat, so the standard rule applies: **All that which can be financialized, *must be* financialized.**

You could think of the electricity-for-sats trade as a *BN;PL scheme* for Bitcoiners…

Because the electricity I burn for sats *today —* some 28 kWh or so; it was warm and calm today — pays me perhaps 2,500 sats *tomorrow morning* (thanks to the wonders of FPPS pools…). But the expense gets recorded by my electricity and distribution companies for November, with the associated fiat invoice due Jan 1 and Jan 7, respectively.

That gets me about 6 weeks of free float. (If I were more degenerate about this, which I *obviously* am, I’d hurl the proceeds into Predyx and buy a safe Nothing Ever Happens  https://stacker.news/items/1602534 short-dated contract for another \~5% return.) Yes, I found the long-awaited answer to *Where does the yield come from?!*

By the logic of time-value-of-money or basic finance, earlier is better. Also, as I wrote in a hopelessly optimistic and bullish [Bitcoin Magazine article years ago](https://bitcoinmagazine.com/culture/dca-effective-going-all-in-on-bitcoin),

> Investing on top of a structurally upward-moving trajectory, a positive-sum game, tilts the stakes in **favor of getting in earlier** (once again, ‘time *in* the market…’).”

Meaning: the sats can appreciate between the moment I earn them and the due date of the fiat liability that created them. Financial fiat alchemy is *on*!

Further, if I swap some of these juicy sats for fiat at a premium to market price, e.g., via peer-to-peer exchanges with a premium https://stacker.news/items/1559053, I can usually bag another couple of percentage points. 
(For all the feds who may or may not be reading, this is of course *totally hypothetical and for illustrative purposes only; not legal or financial advice.*)

In recent years and months, this carry trade hasn’t been an unmitigated *benefit*, with the BTC/USD exchange rate repeatedly dropping like a stone. Still, over time and given that our strong belief in an orange future is correct — certainly something you need to have as a miner/hasher, since the financial benefit of a hashing machine lies mostly in the (far-off) *future* c(h)ash flow it brings — this *should* work out in my favor. Eventually.

## Worth it?

**Yes**. 

I mean, a home miner isn’t a financial decision of the type “I buy this, I’ll make x profit monthly, and by \[purchasing price divided by x] in the future I will have economically paid it off.”

You should start with your own circumstances; assess your own heating needs and how you’re fulfilling those today; what your residential rates are, your potential uptime, and whether there’s something **useful** you can do with the (waste) heat — e.g., heat a sauna or outdoor pool. *Noise?* And also, obviously, what do you think the future of hashprice is? Bitcoin exchange rate? The premium you place on non-KYC sats, or learning about the energy/mining side of things.  

The questions never end. And that is, at least in part, why heatpunkery is so exciting!

*Happy hashing, friends!*

items.title: Trip Report: Santo Domingo
items.text:
Santo Domingo, the capital of the Dominican Republic, is by far the largest metropolitan area in the Caribbean and the oldest continuous colonial settlement in all of the Americas. There are a lot of tourist resorts scattered around the country, but tourism isn't dominating the economy. A lot of sugar, cacao, coffee and tobacco are grown around the island, but there's a robust service and manufacturing industry, too.

Looking purely at BTCMaps, the Dominican Republic seems like one of the few Bitcoin hot spots and given my limited knowledge, I thought the country could be a good candidate for adoption, but as it quickly turned out, most places found on the map do not take Bitcoin, and the country is unlikely to become home to a significant Bitcoin user base.

I focused mainly on exploring the old town, which is somewhat of a magnet for tourists doing day trips from their resorts. Everything in the old town is expensive, and everybody accepts credit cards at no surcharge. Fees don't matter and cards rarely fail. There are plenty of ATMs and currency changers around that "only" charge the usual fees. Wealthy locals might come here for a fancy meal, a wedding or the night clubs. I also ventured outside of the colonial center, and was very impressed by the modern subway system (the only one in the Caribbean) and the two Teleferico (cable car) lines that provide an amazing view of the city.

🍔Roji is a very simple burger joint near the many night clubs. It opens late in the day and is run by a very enthusiastic Bitcoiner who was genuinely happy to see me spending sats, although his assistants at first weren't so sure if I can really pay with Bitcoin. I order the Philly Cheese Steak, which is not too bad, and chat with the owner. I pay to his Blink wallet, which still seems to be using the custodial and reliable Blink node, so my payment goes through quickly at a low fee. The waitress also shows up with her own Blink wallet and asks for a tip, and I happily oblige.

💸The owner at Roji also mentions he is buying and selling Bitcoin from his customers. I offer to buy 1500 DOP, about US$30, all the cash he has in his register. He sells it to me at market rate to his Blink wallet, which I hope wasn't just a favor.

🚬Mercedes Reyes is a beautifully decorated cigar and rum bar with an exciting backstory. It was founded by a Cuban in Frankfurt, Germany and was moved to the Dominican Republic, where they already had a factory. You can come in, chat endlessly with the owners (in Spanish or German), smoke cigars and drink rum. As I arrived the couple owning the place and their son were all gathered in the lobby and not very excited about accepting Bitcoin payments. Only after a while, the son approved and we had to promise to teach them how to accept it. Smoking and drinking in the comfy leather chairs surrounded by antiques was a great pleasure, and I bought some cigars to take with me. As I check out I have to walk the owner through the wallet, which she had set to German. I show her how to set the wallet to Dominican Pesos and request an amount, which feels somewhat hidden in Blink.

🎭Perpetual Lab is a community space. It's one of the few places in the old town that feels genuine and pleasant. On the evening I went there was a pretty cool poetry slam going on, but on another occasion I came for an advertised Bitcoin meetup and found nobody there. Staff didn't hesitate when I wanted to buy a beer with Bitcoin. They looked through their Whatsapp chat history to find a link to the Blink point of sale numpad, which makes the check-out experience so much smoother than the app. There is also a small clothing store at the entrance that accepts Bitcoin, but I couldn't find anything that I wanted to buy there, not even as a gift.

🏷️I didn't find anybody at the Mercado Modolo that accepted Bitcoin, but I still wanted to include it in this list, as it felt like a fairly typical and frustrating experience trying to spend Bitcoin. The market is large but empty, it's built for tourists but is entirely unreachable from the tourist centers. I was pretty much alone inside, bar an army of aggressive touts. Asking about Bitcoin here is pretty much pointless, everybody will enthusiastically say yes and try to lure you into their store. As you try to pay for something they will act confused and try to convince you to pay with pesos, dollars, euros, credit cards, paypal or literally anything other than Bitcoin. They also show zero interest in accepting Bitcoin payments and would rather not make a sale.

There are still a lot of places on BTCMap that I wasn't able to visit and remove. Almost all were verified in 2025, and I doubt any of them accept Bitcoin. Neither locals nor tourists seem to want to spend Bitcoin here, and the Dominican Republic seems to be sufficiently connected financially to not create such demand.

![](https://m.stacker.news/168325)

Sign at Mercedes Reyes accepting Bitcoin payments. The owners however knew nothing about Bitcoin and hesitated to accept it. I might have been the first to spend Bitcoin here.

![](https://m.stacker.news/168326)

Sign at Roji Burgers advertising Bitcoin and Tether to cash exchange.

![](https://m.stacker.news/168327)

![](https://m.stacker.news/168328)

Bitcoin signs at Roji Burgers and the Perpatual Lab.

![](https://m.stacker.news/168329)

View over the city from the Teleferico.

items.title: [Read-along] The Odyssey, W.H.D. Rouse, Books IV - VI
items.text:
*If you've been following along--catch up on the last* [part](https://stacker.news/items/1595925/r/billytheked)*--you probably have found this to be a relaxed pace of reading. Maybe more so than you wish. Alas, life has way of keeping me from this project. As mentioned before, I am reading a hard copy of the translation of W.H.D. Rouse, but I can also recommend the* [*digitized version of the translation of A.S. Kline.*](https://www.poetryintranslation.com/PITBR/Greek/Odhome.php)

***

In the next three books, finally we meet Odysseus, who is (reluctantly?) biding his time on some island with a nymph named Calypso. We hear from his peer, Menelaos and Helen, how Odysseus' heroism and restraint delivered them to victory against the Trojans; however, it becomes harder to distinguish who the true Odysseus really is. His tendency to appear differently from his true nature begins to reveal itself in the stories told about him, and now, first hand, as we are taken along on his adventure to meet the Phaiacians. Thus, we begin to find some truth in the first line of the poem, as translated W.H.D. Rouse, 'here is the story of a man who is never at a loss.' Odysseus begins to earn the name he bears (ὀδύσσομα), whose meaning in Greek translates into something like "to be hated."

## Discussion on Themes

**Hospitality**
The vivid descriptions of feasting, drinking, and making sacrifice to the gods upon the arrival of a guests has defined the escapades of Telemachos up to book IV in the poem. Even as he goes to the house of Menelaos, his good manners and refined appearance precede him, even before he has the chance to make himself known as the son of Odysseus. The Odyssey, being the "national" epic of the Achaeans, takes painstaking effort to provide encyclopedic, lurid descriptions of the level of civilization that had been achieved by Greeks at that time. Clearly, the poem paints a complete and detailed picture of their cultural achievement in the deeply entrenched and refined mores that consistently define what it meant to be Greek. This cultural consistency stands in contrast to the geographic and political separation of the different kingdoms that existed at the time.

**Appearances versus reality**
Finally, in Book V, the reader gets their introduction to Odysseus, who, despite his loyalty to his wife, is on some island playing house with the Nymph Calypso. Since Odysseus rarely presents himself as he truly is, it is impossible for the reader to differentiate whether his desire to return home is authentic, or some hollowed-out sense of moral duty. The reader first learns of his duplicity when Helen recounts how he sneaked into Troy disguised as a beggar, revealing to her their plans to sack the Trojans and rescue her. Also, when Calypso, tells Odysseus he can return home as long as he concedes that his wife is not prettier than her, he lays with her, and doesn't resist. Again, as Odysseus approaches Nausicaa in book VI, he appears as a homeless beggar, in want of proper clothes, when in fact, as we know, Odysseus is the center of attention on Mt Olympus.

**The sea/landscape both as friend and enemy**
There is this sense in the poem that the god of the sea, Earthshaker Poseidon, is the single chaotic force that the Achaeans owe their greatness to, as well as their woes. Nausicaa says to her maids that there is no mortal enemy who do harm on Phaiacia since their country is out of reach, "far away at sea." Also, despite Zeus and Athena's desire to see Odysseus return home, it is grumpy old Poseidon who hurls continued misfortune upon him, as seen after he leaves Calypso. The poem uses the "wine-darkened" sea as a representation of a kind of frontier of civilization, acting at the same time as a buffer of defense, but also a liminal and chaotic realm, where just about anything can happen.

## Questions for contemplation

* **How do you define the frontier of civilization now? Is it a physical place/thing, technological, or something else?**
* **What American national epics document the height of its culture and civilization? How would you characterize these works?**
* **In your opinion, how should we read Odysseus' trickery, as a mark of virtue or a vice?**

# Summaries

## Book IV

Menelaos recounts the death of his brother, Agememnon and laments Odysseus' apparent death, not knowing that he is talking to the latter's very own son. Helen of Troy sedates everyone present with some kind of drug she picked up in Egypt, and tells them the story Odysseus in Troy, where Helen, being held captive, recognized Odysseus disguised as a beggar, who was able to tell her of the Greek's plan to sack the city. Menelaos recounts how he heard her as she circled and touched the Trojan horse, calling our his name, and that if it weren't for Odysseus's being there, urging restraint, he would have called back, blowing their cover. He then tells the story of how he tricked the Old Man of the Sea in Egypt, disguising himself and two of his men with seal carcasses so they can ambush him while he is asleep. The Old Man tells Menelaos of Agememnon's murder, and how Odysseus was still living. Penelope, back in Ithica, prays to Athena, as her suitors plot against Telemachos, laying in wait for his ships to return. Athena summons the ghost of Iphthime, daughter of Icarus, to visit Athena in her sleep to inform her that she will protect Telemachos from harm.

## Book V

Zeus and Athena discuss Odysseus' fate. Zeus reluctantly agrees to intervene to by sending Hermes to inform Calypso of their desire to see Odysseus find his way home, on the condition that Odysseus travel without man or god, and only after a good dose of bad fortune. Calpyso tells Hermes that she loves Odysseus, but does not wish to anger Zeus. She tells Odysseus that it is the god's will that he be allowed to go home, but that he must admit she is prettier than his wife, which he does, and the sleeps with her. Calypso send him off, helping him to hew trees and craft a ship, supplies him with food and wine and water. Poseidon sees Odysseus thus returning, close to his destiny, and decides on shaking up his world, sending a storm his way, to throw him off course. Ino, or Leucothea, the White Sea Goddess, takes pity on him, orders him to strip his clothes and gives him a veil that helps him swim to safety. At first Odysseus refuses, choosing to test his fate and his trusted raft, but this quickly shatters like straw on the threshing floor, and he takes Ino's advice. After he swims to safety, he kisses the earth, returns the veil to Ino, prays to Zeus, and finds a place to take shelter, collapsing from exhaustion.

## Book VI

In the house of Alcinoos, king of the Phaiacians, sleeps his daughter, Nausicaa. Athena visits her in a dream to inspire her to take all of her best bridal linens down to the river to be washed, for the time is coming when she must be prepared to be wed. Thus, Nausicaa appeals to her father, who allows this, prepares for her carts and donkeys. She and her maids take the linens down to a rushing stream, bathe, lather in olive oil, and adorn themselves as the goddess Artemis, daughter of Zeus. They begin playing ball, when Athena decides that it is time that Odysseus is awaken. She causes one of them to drop the ball, sending it hurling down toward the eddies, awakening him. He emerges, craggy and briny, approaches the women, all who get scared away except for Nausicaa, whose fear Athena removed. Odysseus, impressed by her refinement, makes an appeal to her for clothes, which she agrees to. He washes and changes, and Athena makes him taller and more handsome. Finally, the latter invites Odysseus to return to Phaiacia among her party, instructing him to hide in her father's orchard until she makes it back to her father's house. She gives him instructions on how to find her, and tells him he must supplicate himself to her mother if he wishes to return to his own people.

items.title: Linklater's film Slacker (1991): Radical and Mediocre
items.text:
# On this fine day in Austin, TX, I got Linklater'ed.

It doesn't happen often, but I can count on it when Linklater made it. Can I even describe it? It's like this: you see a film, and then you live in that world for the rest of the day. You found it so comfortable and novel there, that reality colors your vision for a while, a constructed reality, sure (and eventually you'll settle back into what you know as reality, because it is unnatural for reality to bend into one shape for too long).

I've seen several Linklater films, most notably the *Before* trilogy and *Boyhood*. So when I heard a film enthusiast describe *Slacker*, I knew it would be the kind of thing I'd take to, no problem. Plus, filmed in the city I live in more than 30 years ago, I was looking forward to spotting familiar landmarks and marveling at landscape changes. And that is part of the experience I really enjoyed, but then another part of my mind has been captured by the film, and I am unable now to steer it away, so I've come here to write about it.

That's the thing with Linklater, I find. You don't just casually see these films. There's an incubation period once it's over. It's integrating itself into you. There's a heavy dose of culturally-relevant mind-melding technology in whatever he's doing with the pictures on the screen, the characters on display. Today I found out how hungry I have been for this kind of entertainment.

## about the film

> [*Slacker*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slacker_(film)) follows a single day in the life of an ensemble of mostly under-30 [bohemians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohemianism "Bohemianism") and misfits in [Austin, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin,_Texas "Austin, Texas"). The film follows various eccentric and misfit characters and scenes, never staying with one character or conversation for more than a few minutes before moving on to someone else in the scene and following them.

![](https://m.stacker.news/167045)
^ that's Rick kicking off the whole thing with talk of strange dreams

> The characters include a talkative taxi passenger (played by Linklater), a [UFO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unidentified_flying_object "Unidentified flying object") [buff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fan_(aficionado) "Fan (aficionado)") who insists the U.S. has been on the [moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon") since the 1950s, a [JFK conspiracy theorist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy_assassination_conspiracy_theories "John F. Kennedy assassination conspiracy theories"), an elderly [anarchist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anarchy "Anarchy") who befriends a man trying to rob his house, a [television set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_set "Television set") [collector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collecting "Collecting"), and a woman trying to sell a [Madonna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madonna_(entertainer) "Madonna (entertainer)") [pap smear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pap_test "Pap test").

![](https://m.stacker.news/167049)

> Other characters include a woman hiding a black eye behind sunglasses who offers a random pick of [Oblique Strategies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oblique_Strategies "Oblique Strategies") to passers-by, a young man who perhaps accidentally or perhaps intentionally has run over his mother with the family car, three renters in a rooming house who discover and read a pack of postcards on the floor of a fellow renter who has moved out, a young woman who has just arrived back in town after her parents put her in a mental hospital in [Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas "Dallas"), and a man who tries to convince a friend to throw a tent and a typewriter into a creek to reject an ex-girlfriend symbolically.

![](https://m.stacker.news/167050)

![](https://m.stacker.news/167051)

## on being bohemian

I'm responding to the film because I'm identifying with it, and I'm nostalgic for it. The perfect cocktail for a lingering rumination of conceivable significance. I'll be nursing my headache in the morning.

See, I'm a collector, right? And my favorite objects are characters, people who've got something to say, something you could never anticipate, predict, or expect. When I've been passive observer of the grungy art and music scene, I find it as thrilling as riding a rollercoaster. And there have been periods of my life where I've gotten to live out a type of bohemian fantasy, like where people aren't really people, but characters. Each one offering me an interesting scrap that I'll capture in some way. And Linklater made a movie out of this pastime.

But where are these characters now? I can't find them in Austin in 2026. Now, you catch up with your buddy's band passing through to play a show, and all the bandmates scatter across east Austin searching for and finding drugs. And you follow them to make sure nothing bad happens, and they just wanna eat, and they don't say anything interesting. Or you throw a house party for the first time in ages and people stand around discussing ROI and you get so depressed by that. Or you go to an art show opening and no one is relaxed enough to even look you in the eyes, the room's so stuffed with self-importance. Or you made too many jokes poking fun at gay people and now your friends won't invite you out to see their gay plays which you find out later are really sucky anyway. I don't know, I ramble on. I'm just complaining because I miss freaks.

I miss the sensation of standing in front of a stranger and having no clue what might come out of their mouth. That sensation is the main character of *Slacker*.

## what is radical is mediocre

Turning to a different observation of the film, now that my personal confession is out of the way, there's a funny irony in the sincerity of this character's passionate convictions and the fact that their all slackers. For example, the climactic moment that a gun is pulled out in a robbery, the tension it introduces is immediately dissolved by the friendly banter of an aging man. The robber went in with the gun, right, but couldn't commit himself to the use of it, so he takes the cup of coffee offered to him. It's a little silly. It's a special silliness that belongs to sincere people who over-identify themselves with a political idea. And that happens to be a lot of bohemians, or leftists as we now know them. But that term doesn't capture the misfits, the unpopular weirdos pursuing uncomfortable hobbies, the harmless conspiracy-theorists, those who believe in something radical but live sheltered in mediocrity. Is that an expressly American thing? And did these people stop existing recently when they found out their uniqueness, nothing more, could be made profitable online?

I wonder about that, and a few other things.

Ah, another thing I loved about this film, not a drop of makeup anywhere to be seen.

items.title: Nathan Pinkoski's Introduction to "The Camp of the Saints" by Jean Raspail
items.text:
If you've never heard of the book *The Camp of the Saints*, you're not alone.  Widely maligned as a racist screed, it's a 1973 dystopian novel by award-winning French author Jean Raspail that tells the tale of an armada transporting a million migrants from India to the shores of France, throwing the country into social chaos.  The novel predicts, almost a tee, the modern reactions and counter-reactions to mass migration in Western Europe and America.  Because of its unflattering depiction of immigrants and the consequences of mass migration, its print run in English was limited, and it wasn't until recently that a revised English translation became widely available.

I heard of the book through my watching of videos by Raymond Ibrahim, another person often maligned as racist and Islamophobic.  By revealing the kinds of people I watch and the kinds of books I read, I suppose I am outing myself as a potential bigot, but in my defense I'll offer that I read books [critical of Western imperialism](https://stacker.news/items/1405134) as well.

I decided to pick up the 2025 English translation by Vauban books, which contains a nice introduction by Nathan Pinkoski, an American conservative intellectual.  I was so impressed by the introduction that I decided to post selected excerpts from it here for stackers to read.    Hope it triggers some interesting discussion and some interest in the book.

`<begin Pinkoski>`

***

## Introduction

You are holding in your hands one of the most important dystopian novels ever written.

But unlike Aldous Huxley’s Brave New World and George Orwell’s 1984, Jean Raspail’s The Camp of the Saints lacks any aura of respectability. In the United States, it is attacked as a bigoted screed, “a must-read within white supremacist circles.” Raspail, who won some of France’s most important literary prizes, is regarded as an outright racist rather than as an accomplished writer. This narrative has stood for years in large part because the publishing houses that owned the rights to the English translation have suppressed the book. That is why the authorized release of this new edition by Robert Laffont, the French publishing house that owns the original rights, is so important. For the first time in many years, English-speakers have unrestricted access to the text, brought to life in Ethan Rundell’s vivid new translation. English-language audiences can now finally understand Raspail’s hypnotic and haunting tale and appreciate why the novel remains of lasting significance.

Huxley’s Brave New World and Orwell’s 1984 show how the assumptions of self-satisfied materialism, far from building a progressive paradise, can underwrite a permanent political nightmare. Describing fully achieved dystopias, the novels capture two sides of modern despotism: one, soft and seductive; the other, hard and brutal. The Camp of the Saints, by contrast, divulges a dystopia as it comes to be. It explores the implications of modern spiritual self-hatred.

The central plot concerns an armada that transports a million migrants from India to the shores of France, throwing the country and the West into chaos. But The Camp of the Saints is not a disaster novel. The book’s importance does not hinge on whether Raspail was correct in predicting mass immigration or in describing it in catastrophic terms. Rather, the novel’s genius lies in the depiction of an apocalypse in the original sense of that term. Properly translated, apocalypse means revelation, disclosure – literally, an “uncovering.” The Camp of the Saints, whose title is taken from the Book of Revelation, unveils the perverse logic that pervades late Western civilization, throwing into sharp relief the nihilism of guilt. Too spiritually weak to appreciate their own distinction and to defend themselves, Westerners welcome their own destruction under the guise of creating a perfect world cleansed of their past sins.

When interpreted by careless critics – and they are legion – The Camp of the Saints is about a fictional race war, a device for stoking fears about genocide against whites. This is the standard reading of both racialists and progressives. But for decades, thoughtful people could discuss other interpretations. National Review and The Atlantic published sober, sympathetic essays on The Camp of the Saints by distinguished scholars.4 Those days are gone. There’s little hope that those steeped in progressive lore will take this novel seriously. And many American conservatives now enforce the rules of reading set by the Left. Even in the few remaining institutions they control, conservatives are constantly fearful of progressive reproaches. In their quixotic bids to charm the same leftists who hate them, conservatives purge their ranks and turn on their friends. The reader of this book should be warned: to talk about The Camp of the Saints, still less to take it seriously and defend it, is not for the faint of heart. You must be prepared to pay the price.

Those who are anxious about The Camp of the Saints fixate on passages in which Raspail describes the migrants as primitive and barbaric; they see this as evidence that the book is a white supremacist tract. But this reading misses the point of the novel. Raspail is holding a mirror up to Western society: he is concerned with “us,” not “them.” Moreover, the attempt to slander Raspail and his work as the incarnation of white supremacy betrays a profound ignorance of Raspail’s life and vocation as the literary voice of the world’s forgotten peoples.

## Biography

\[*Here, Pinkoski gives a biography of Raspail, primarily to show that he most certainly was NOT racist by any means, but rather admired cultures different from his own.  Raspail's purpose in writing The Camp of the Saints was to explore whether Europe could lose its culture like other cultures before it.  Here are selected excerpts from the biography*]

...

The journey clarified Raspail’s vocation. Discovering an abandoned Algonquin village on an island in Lake Huron, Raspail received one of the decisive shocks of his life. “I remember my emotion,” he wrote, “as if I entered into a church and rediscovered my faith.” An awe for the world’s almost-vanished tribes guided him thereafter. The crew spent the night in the middle of the village, though without raising their flag – guests of the place’s original occupants, not conquerors. Later on during their journey, Raspail met a man, “Bill,” who chided him and his friends for their naïve Indianisme. “In Europe,” he told them, “dreams of the past take up too much place in your life. Here, we don’t talk of the past, but of the dam and the hydroelectric plant.” Raspail’s whole literary career could be described as a revolt against this attitude. Countering those who spurn the past and hail technological conformity, Raspail told the stories of disappearing peoples whom progressives consigned to extinction.

...

Raspail’s best novels are an unusual kind of historical fiction. They encompass historical events that veer off into the realm of fantasy, of historical counterfactuals that recount the sudden resurfacing of long-lost dynasties or peoples. L’Anneau du pêcheur (The Ring of the Fisherman) envisages the resurgent lineage of the Avignon papacy. Qui se souvient des hommes … (Who will remember the people …), portrays the Alakalufs; on the cusp of extinction, their language has no word for happiness, but hundreds to express suffering. Pêcheur de lunes (Fisher of Moons) depicts the remnants of the Ainu of Northern Japan and Russia. Sire, a kind of theological thriller, imagines a king of France crowned in contemporary Europe, as the regalia of the lost Arthurian world reemerge. Like other twentieth-century European writers, Raspail enjoyed mixing real and fictitious places, often gesturing toward the old, vanishing Europe. Hergé created a new monarchy in the Balkans, Syldavia, for Tintin to explore. It harkened back to the ancient monarchies of pre-1914 Europe. Raspail imagined a new Central European principality, Altheim-Neufra. It also harkened back to the stabilities of aristocratic Europe, lost after the world wars.

Two themes pervade Raspail’s work. One is a literary royalism. Raspail offers up monarchy not as a readily applicable political program, but rather as a transcendent, poetic refuge from the banality of modern politics. It captures at once a regret for what is lost, a defiance of the follies of the present, and a dream for what may come. The other theme is love for places and peoples distant in time and space. This love shapes Raspail’s determination to transmit the memory of almost vanished nations. Sometimes it led him to deliver particularly harsh tirades against the present. Modern New York, he judged, was “a desert” because “we no longer run into an Algonquin.”14 Chanting this polyphonic hymn to the nobility and fragility of the world’s peoples, Raspail affirms the particularity of cultures and civilizations. There’s no agenda in him for imposing Western norms across the globe. The world cannot be refitted into the model of the “dam and the hydroelectric plant.” Had Raspail kept his study of indigenous tribes to the far-off places unfamiliar to most Westerners, he might have preserved an unblemished reputation as a novelist and writer with arguably anti-colonialist sympathies.

Yet in one early work, he committed an unpardonable offense. He wondered whether the fate of the indigenous peoples of Europe would be similar to the peoples who had vanished in the wake of European colonization. Now, as Europeans retreated from their empires, were they just as vulnerable, just as liable to vanish from history – and just as deserving of a lament? Sometime in the 1960s and 70s, such thinking became taboo. And so for better or for worse, all of Raspail’s literary oeuvre is now measured by the one novel that took up those questions and imagined the end of European and Western civilization.

## The Novel

\[*Here, Pinkoski offers his analysis of the novel. It is full of spoilers, so I will only post some spoiler-free excerpts here*.]

...

The ethic of decolonization trades off the utopian vision of multicultural progressivism, which assumes that everyone in the world can be incorporated into a single rainbow regime. Yet the universalism underlying this project masks its coercive, dystopic dimension. Raspail pulls aside the mask. Multicultural progressivism demands the subjugation and destruction of all traditional forms of life. Its prime target is the West because the engine that drives it is Western cowardice and self-hatred; multiculturalism is the cultural imperialism of European self-loathing. Such impulses are masked by belief in the atoning power of capitulation to mass immigration and the deconstruction of European identity. But Raspail knows the truth: immigrants do not have the power to deliver Europeans from their sense of worthlessness. Once one embraces the logic of civilizational repudiation, the endpoint is nihilism and cultural death. The Alpha is European guilt. The Omega is Eurocide.

The plot of The Camp of the Saints is fantasy, but it is not frivolous. By the 1980s, those able to perceive the trajectory of European and French society saw that the novel could not be dismissed. Mitterrand thanked Raspail for sending him the book, which he promised to read “with much interest.” Jospin thanked Raspail for writing the book, “which describes a future that is not,” which is to say: a future that was in the process of happening. As the shadow of political correctness descended upon French intellectual life, leftists who could never praise the book in public did so in private. In 2004, Denis Olivennes, who managed the French left-wing daily Libération, wrote to Raspail: “Thirty years ago, I would have undoubtedly considered The Camp of the Saints as a despicable polemic.” But since reading it, “not only do I no longer hate those who do not think like me, I’m interested in them!” Robert Badinter, the Jewish socialist Minister of Justice, a champion of international human rights law who abolished the death penalty in France, thanked Raspail for the 1985 edition. “Ten years ago I read it with great interest,” he wrote. “With the flow of time the problem has become more pressing … The civilization which is ours is only threatened from the inside, more by losing its soul than by yielding to external demographic pressures.”

Badinter discerned that we are imperiled above all by Western civilization’s own internal spiritual crisis. This insight is what now makes The Camp of the Saints so disturbing to read. The desire to make ourselves culturally prostrate has come into the open.

...

Raspail was concerned to do more than unveil that spiritual death of the West. The Camp of the Saints offers guidance to those of us who hope to save our spiritual integrity as we seek to preserve and honor our patrimony. It shows us how not to act. The novel’s band of resisters, though patriots who love their country and culture, are very much part of Raspail’s satire. At best, they practice a simple postwar Epicureanism, appreciating the quotidian pleasures afforded by their country’s prosperity, customs, and culinary traditions. At worst, they lack ethical refinement and display a rough, schoolboy Nietzscheanism. They are lovers of sensual pleasures but they are also lovers of violence. They have only the fragments of the real religion. They are Last Men.

The tragic center of the novel is a civilization pulled between two portals of death. On the one hand, there is an eschatological universalism, premised on the unique guilt of one civilization, which makes the collective suicide of the West a spiritual duty. On the other hand, there is a raw particularism, which may animate the community, but leaves its members bereft of pity and mercy and so devoid of any authentic spirituality. For Christians, the novel poses a dilemma. Either uphold a natural love of home and country and reject Christianity; or uphold Christianity but reject the natural love of home and country.

...

We in the West are in thrall to a false dilemma between universalism and particularism. It may be the specific charism of French Catholicism to overcome it. This is a charism that can heal a world where the old Christian virtues have gone mad, guiding the Church to recover the fullness of her treasures and helping the baptized nations of the West save their souls.

Whatever the ultimate theological resolution may be, Raspail’s later works are literary explorations that take us beyond the novel’s dilemma. Just like The Camp of the Saints, these are novels about cultural destruction that imagine what survivors and resisters must do after the catastrophe has occurred. Just like The Camp of the Saints, they describe little platoons of resisters who try to save a culture threatened with extinction, to protect the fragile roots of traditions touched by the deep frost of modernity. Yet it is these survivors, these devotees of a cause and creed assaulted by the Great and the Good, who in the later novels practice an ethic of friendship and cultivate genuine fortitude. They rarely win. Their numbers diminish and their historic territories are lost. But their very resistance, along with the spiritual integrity it attests to, assures the transmission of what is noble, even if those who endure must go underground for centuries. They bury their dead, but not to forget them; they bury their dead with the hope of seeing them rise again.

Reading and defending The Camp of the Saints is not unlike enrolling in one of these little platoons. They are acts of defiance, refusals to submit to the stolid conventions and anemic conformism that dictate the lives of fearful, lesser men. The motive is not mere contrarianism, but the realization that a valuable treasure has been subject to unjust calumnies or condemnations and stands at risk of disappearing forever. We act to stop that disappearance from happening and to save our spiritual heritage. The fruits of these battles are elusive. The penalties for standing firm and fighting on are steep. But to suffer them is a badge of honor.

***

items.title: The Open Study Hubs
JoinMarket Feeder Coinjoins — Kruw | bitcoin++ Seoul, privacy edition
