items.text:
I'm vibe coding the prototype here: [https://github.com/Kruwed/BlackHole](https://github.com/Kruwed/BlackHole)

Thank you for attending my presentation today. My name is Kruw. I'm a contributor to Wasabi Wallet and my npub is up there in that QR code in case you want to find me on Nostr later.

Today I'm going to be talking about incentivizing privacy on Bitcoin's base layer. So the talk we just saw with cross input signature aggregation also helps with that. We got to see how fees could be saved for miners. But mine is more of like an economic game, and I'm calling it JoinMarket "Feeder" coinjoin.

So there's two main strategies used by blockchain analysts to link addresses together on chain. The first is the common input ownership heuristic which assumes that when a transaction contains multiple inputs that they all originate from the same sender's wallet.

And the other assumption is when a transaction creates two outputs, only one of those belongs to the intended payment recipient and the other one is just used to recycle the leftover value back into the sender's wallet. And we call this a change output.

So even though there's five unique addresses in this transaction, we would interpret this as only two parties. There's one sender, one receiver, and the sender actually controls four out of five of those addresses.

So we can defeat these assumptions by constructing collaborative transactions called coinjoins. This five input transaction actually contains inputs from five different users wallets. And to protect each other's privacy, each of these participants is going to create an output with a matching value.

So I've highlighted these on the output side. Five out of the nine outputs create an amount of exactly 489,410 satoshis. So this matching property makes it so that observers would only have a 20% chance of correctly guessing which one of these outputs came from any one of these specific inputs.

So the framework used to construct this transaction is called JoinMarket and it's an incentive aligned protocol that where taker where takers who are seeking privacy collaborate with makers who are seeking profits. There's some additional mechanisms called fidelity bonds and poodles that I'm not going to go into detail with today, but the purpose is to exclude dishonest participants from participating in this market.

So the same coinjoin that we saw before, we can't rely on the common input ownership heuristic. So I've broken it down into this little spreadsheet. And the purpose here is for me to try and identify who the taker of the transaction is and pull him apart from all the makers that he's paying.

And you know I ran the numbers and it was this guy with the input for 500,000 Satoshi's. He was the taker and he paid a little bit over 10,000 sats and fees to miners and to the makers for their liquidity. And in exchange for footing this bill, he gets privacy on 100% of his balance. There's no change output created for him and he gets there's no trust involved.

But the other four participants, they have leftover coins that weren't fully anonymized. So those change outputs will still point backwards to the inputs they came from, but they still gain privacy on part of their balance.

Unfortunately, despite this method being around for over a decade, only a small minority of Bitcoin transactions are enhancing their privacy by coin joining. And whenever I ask Bitcoiners, you know, why are you sending a solo payment? Why aren't you coinjoining? These are the two top responses I get from critics.

The first is that they're concerned about the long-term efficacy of the coinjoin privacy. If another participant in this transaction went and consolidated their coins later, then it would deanonymize themselves and then also reduce the privacy for everyone else in the group.

And the other concern is about the fungibility of private outputs, because merchants or exchanges that use like an automated blacklist might confuse you for someone else and then reject your payment.

But I think both of these problems can be solved by applying economic pressure so that both senders and receivers are always incentivized to coinjoin. So I want to introduce a new concept called anonymity points to apply this pressure. And don't panic, it's not a shitcoin. It's just an abstraction that we use for price discovery. So my goal is to attach extra value to coinjoin outputs which would then impose an artificial cost on anyone who forfeits that privacy.

So how do we capture AP value? Well, unlike units of Bitcoin which are inherited by the descendants of a transaction, an output's AP value gets destroyed when it's spent. But this is okay because the AP value from the ancestor transaction gets overwritten by the AP value of the descendant transaction. So this lets us simulate a swap where coin join participants either pay sats for AP or receive sats, based on the points difference between the ancestor transaction they're leaving from and the descendant transaction they're entering into.

So how does this approach differ from classic joint market coinjoins? Well, instead of makers charging a percentage fee or a flat fee for their liquidity, makers post an exchange rate that they're willing to buy an anonymity points for.

But since a taker's coinjoin might end up producing more anonymity points than the maker already had, they also need to list the exchange rate that they're willing to buy points for. But makers can still guarantee a profit through arbitrage just by setting a higher selling price than their buying price.

So this is what the maker order book might look like. Makers would post the lowest mining fee rate that they're willing to tolerate, the rate that they're purchasing points for and the rate that they're selling points for. And then takers would wait until there's enough attractive offers that have accumulated in the order book and then build a huge coin join transaction to produce and sell points.

So how do we measure a transaction's AP value? We count the number of inputs that are being remixed from a previous coinjoin. We count the number of outputs that are being matched in the current coin join. And then we take the lower of those two values. Then we assign that amount to all the matched outputs in the new transaction. And an output that doesn't have any matches doesn't gain any points.

So this is the same five input coin join that we looked at earlier except I went back and looked up the scores and actually only Alice had any score on the input that she's submitting in this transaction. Her input is worth two anonymity points, but the new output she received is only worth one anonymity point.

So this means that the taker is going to have to compensate her at her selling rate for the amount of points that she gave up. But these other three makers, well, none of them started with any points and they ended up gaining one point from this transaction. So they have to pay out at the buy rate that they listed to the taker a small amount of sats for increasing their privacy. And so the taker here their net result is plus9 satoshi's. I just kind of made up these rates. They might not be realistic but he actually gains from basically being a coordinator of this coin join and finding a bunch of people who increase their privacy.

So, who pays for the mining fees? In a classic joinmarket coinjoin, the taker pays for everything. Pays for all the inputs, all the outputs, and the transaction overhead. And I've rounded these numbers here. A normal taproot input costs 57.5 vbytes, but it's really pretty number when you add both together, and it's 100. So, I just left it like that. But in a feeder joinmarket coinjoin makers are actually responsible for paying for inputs or outputs that don't contribute to anonymity points. And to prevent points from being wasted, there's an additional penalty imposed on takers. If they create a change output for a maker, they have to front them an extra 57 vbytes worth of mining fees because the maker will need to consume that later to get back into the pool.

And then also there's some flexibility here. We can actually allow makers to batch their own payments into the coin join opportunistically at a very cheap rate. So this is what our five input coinjoin looks like. Now instead of having four change outputs, there's only one change output for the largest whale who we've named Charlie. The all the rest of the balance gets broken down into matching outputs, but only pairs of two in this case. So this is the most cost-effective way for the taker to generate points and avoid creating change outputs.

items.title: Austin trip day six: lakes, hikes, final bitcoin meal.
items.text:
Hey stackers,

I write from the airport terminal in route to the chilly easy coast. What an incredible trip this has been. I’m normally looking forward to getting back home and returning to the recurrence of every day life. Not this time. I am not ready to leave and I know I’ll be back. Perhaps to live one day.

Yesterday morning I woke up at 3 AM a little hung over from all my wine at III forks and I couldn’t sleep. So I went to play poker. Got there at 4 AM and the crowd was wild. Everyone had been there since the night before and everyone seemed drunk, tired, or both. I played this huge hand and ended up winning a $1400 pot. https://stacker.news/items/1606387/r/SatAttack?commentId=1606424

I played until about 7 AM and headed out for breakfast. I ended up at a really nice diner called Phoebes diner and had a great meal. Forgot take pictures though. They sell slab bacon and serve it in thick deep fried slices. Wonderful. I get back to the hotel and sleep from 830AM to 12PM. @grayruby had recommended I take the 30 minute drive to visit lake Travis. After poking around on my phone for things around there I found a hike and a restaurant I wanted to do.

Here’s the all trail for the hike: [river place nature trail](https://www.alltrails.com/trail/us/texas/river-place-canyon-trail?sh=true)

The hike ended up being a great success. The weather was great and it was just the right amount of challenging to get the heart pumping.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164323)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164324)

I’ll take a little time to plug the Earth Runners here. For all my barefoot maxis out there this is a wonderful footwear for rocky environments where bare feet may have a tough time. I have taken these everywhere in all sorts of terrain. Love them.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164326)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164327)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164328)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164329)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164330)

Awesome hike. I was pleased to find good water flow and was surprised how clear it was! That tree going across the path is called the noggin knocker and there was a sign warning you not to knock your noggin haha.

Finishing my hike I was very ready for food and water and headed out to a restaurant right on Lake Travis called The Oasis. I didn’t really know what I was getting myself into but this place was GRAND. It’s a massive four story restaurant that’s the size of a big hotel. All four stories have a balcony that over looks the lake. There’s awesome art and decorations everywhere.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164331)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164332)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164333)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164334)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164335)

On my way in there was this blue metal UFO thing covered in stickers. I took the opportunity to put one of the stickers @k00b gave me on there. Turned out nice I think.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164336)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164337)

The food was decent. I got the chips and salsa. (Great chips!!) the chicken enchiladas with rice and beans, and a margarita on the rocks. I wasn’t planning on drinking but… the view made me.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164338)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164339)

I got back to my hotel around 6 pm and slept until 830. I had been deliberating between going to play poker one last time or going to find one last place to spend some sats. The issue was they were in opposite directions and I was really torn for a while. With one last check of BTCmaps I found a great solution. A place called Rockin Rolls that wasn’t in the downtown areas! It was close enough to the hotel and poker room to do both. So off I went. Here’s the BTCmap link [https://btcmap.org/merchant/node:13309320506](https://btcmap.org/merchant/node:13309320506)
It’s a small food truck in small gathering of food trucks right off the road. I appreciated the abundance of parking here!

![](https://m.stacker.news/164342)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164343)

These guys are awesome and if you’re a pizza eater in Austin I recommend giving this one a try. They make sourdough pizza rolls and they are very good. I ordered three classics (pepperoni and cheese) and a mini cannoli. Now time to pay. I see they only have the small white square terminal and I won’t be presented with the toggle option so I tell the man I’d like to pay with bitcoin if I can… he isn’t sure and calls the owner over who was thankfully there. He says “I think I set that up …” and we collectively poke around the terminal. Doesn’t take us long to find Bitcoin listed as one of the payment options and I tell them all we have to do is click that and it should generate me a QR code. It did and I made another seemless Phoenix payment. I gave my small spiel about how cool this is and how anyone who knows how can interact with this terminal with a bunch of different options.

The owner, Jake, was impressed and pleased. He was excited to see bitcoin being used and told me I was the first to do it. But on BTCmaps someone had verified the location in November 2025 so I was thinking perhaps not. I showed him BTCmaps and his little page on there and he thought that was very cool too! I told him that I would be blogging about this day and experience on stacker news and gave him the lowdown about what goes on here. “That sounds right my ally” he said. He loves community and according to him he likes crypto. He’s an ethereum guy he says. I told him I don’t know anything about it because I haven’t been able to move past Bitcoin. I was explaining what SN was and he understood immediately. “So instead of a like you just send over a little satoshi?” YEAH! I gave him a SN sticker and told him how to find us and that if he ever had any questions or inquires about using bitcoin in his business or other wise this is the place to come. I told him he would be very welcomed as a business owner accepting sats.

When I got my order I realized I didn’t have a drink. I asked for a bottle of water and had opened my Phoenix wallet to pay but he just said don’t worry about it. Thanks Jake!

I’ll say again, if you like pizza, come try this place. It’s awesome and he was telling me he’s looking to move to another state. Him and his wife love Austin but they’ve been there for 20 years and are ready for change. So time is running out!

![](https://m.stacker.news/164347)

After my pizza rolls it was time for one last poker sesh. I headed back to the lodge card club and played an uneventful 1.5 hours and won $10. I got gas for  the Turo rental, got to my hotel around 1130, and packed up. I had to be up at 530 to head to the airport.

I enjoyed my time in Austin very much and I really enjoyed sharing my experience here on stackers!! I’ve gotten a lot of support and a lot of engagement and that has been sweet. Thanks for reading and thank you to those who gave me awesome suggestions. I tried to do them all.

If you missed the other trip reports here they are:

Day one:
https://stacker.news/items/1602995/r/SatAttack

Day two: https://stacker.news/items/1603699/r/SatAttack

Day three: https://stacker.news/items/1604324/r/SatAttack

Day four and five: https://stacker.news/items/1605873/r/SatAttack

items.title: Tether Fun Unbelievable Details - Part VI
items.text:
*This is part of a larger series on the history of Tether. Part I (*https://stacker.news/items/1042943*), Part II (*https://stacker.news/items/1059310*), Part III (*https://stacker.news/items/1115791*), Part IV (*https://stacker.news/items/1410689/*), Part V (*https://stacker.news/items/1613156*)*

# 19 CANTOR FITZGERALD

19.1   On 1 December 2021, Rumble Inc., [announces](https://www.cantor.com/rumble-inc-the-neutral-video-platform-to-go-public-through-combination-with-cantor-fitzgeralds-cf-acquisition-corp-vi-nasdaq-cfvi/) it will go public through combination with Cantor Fitzgerald's CF Acquisition Corp. VI.

19.11   "Rumble is designed to be the rails and independent infrastructure that is immune to cancel culture. We are a movement that does not stifle, censor, or punish creativity and believe everyone benefits from access to a neutral network with diverse ideas and opinions. We are on a mission to restore the internet to its roots by making it free and open once again. The transaction we announced today will provide Rumble with the additional capital necessary to continue to scale our business and carry out our mission." [--Chris Pavlovski, Founder and CEO of Rumble](https://www.cantor.com/rumble-inc-the-neutral-video-platform-to-go-public-through-combination-with-cantor-fitzgeralds-cf-acquisition-corp-vi-nasdaq-cfvi/)

19.111   "The CF VI Board has unanimously approved and adopted the Business Combination Agreement and unanimously recommends that our stockholders vote “FOR” each of the Proposals presented to CF VI Stockholders." [-Amendment No. 1 to Form 2-4 Registration Statement under the Securities Act of 1933 for CF Acquisition Corp. VI](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1830081/000121390022026101/fs42022a1_cfacquisition6.htm)

19.12   Howard Lutnick [says](https://www.cantor.com/rumble-inc-the-neutral-video-platform-to-go-public-through-combination-with-cantor-fitzgeralds-cf-acquisition-corp-vi-nasdaq-cfvi/) "Rumble is the most exciting social media and video distribution platform in the market today."

19.13   "Today Rumble enters a new era. We partnered with Tether, a company that exports American values to the entire world, and who are major advocates for free speech." [--Chris Pavlovski](https://x.com/chrispavlovski/status/1870249250241511654)

19.131   Rumble [announces](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1830081/000121390024111298/ea022562201ex99-1_rumble.htm) $775 million strategic investment from Tether.

19.132   "Most people don't realize Tether is a Bitcoin company that happens to do other things like Ai, energy, and stablecoins." [--Samson Mow](https://x.com/Excellion/status/1870577229367005648)

19.133   "Beyond our initial shareholder stake, Tether intends to drive towards a meaningful advertising, cloud, and crypto payment solutions relationship with Rumble." [--Paolo Ardoino](https://www.rum.group/blog/rumble-announces-775-million-strategic-investment-from-tether/)

19.134   "Tether deeply believes in the fundamental values of freedom of speech and financial freedom." [--Paolo Ardoino](https://x.com/paoloardoino/status/1870231681497538759)

19.135   Rumble [closes](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1830081/000121390025011371/ea023027801ex99-1_rumble.htm) the $775 million strategic investment from Tether on 7 February 2025.

19.14   Tether's 2023 Q4 attestation [reports](https://tether.io/news/tethers-2023-q4-attestation/) $2.85 billion in profit.

19.2   "There's a company that I like called Tether." [-Howard Lutnick](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/videos/2024-01-16/lutnick-the-fed-is-staying-higher-for-longer-video)

19.21   "I manage many, many of their assets. And Tether Holdings is the name of the group, And the group, from what we've seen, and we did a lot of work, they have the money they say they have. In the last attestation they said they had $86 billion of assets and $83 billion of liabilities, and I've seen and the firm has seen a whole lot and they have the money. So there's always been a lot of talk saying 'Do they have it or not?' so I'm with you guys saying, 'We've seen it. And they have it.'" [-Howard Lutnick](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/videos/2024-01-16/lutnick-the-fed-is-staying-higher-for-longer-video)

19.211   "I basically told him the movie line. I said, ‘Show me the money,’" Lutnick told a crypto conference in July. "And we found every penny, and they had every penny, but they had it in what I would call pretty godforsaken places," he said, noting Tether’s holdings of short-term loans to Chinese companies, known as commercial paper. [-Howard Lutnick in *The Wall Street Journal*](https://archive.is/rSRx1#selection-5681.0-5681.330)

19.2111   On 10 February 2023, The Wall Street Journal [reports](https://archive.is/4wyww) that Cantor Fitzgerald helps oversee Tether's $39 billion in Treasury holdings.

19.212   The Wall Street Journal also [reports](https://archive.is/4wyww) that Tether "began moving its reserves into the Wall Street brokerage in late 2021, around the time it reached a settlement with a regulator, one of the people said."

19.2121   And [that](https://archive.is/4wyww) Cantor is one of the 25 so-called primary dealers for the U.S. Treasurys market, a status that allows them to trade directly with the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and underwrite sales of U.S. government debt.

19.213   "Tether and Cantor had established a relationship in 2021 when Cantor began acting as a custodian and trading partner for a portion of the U.S. treasuries backing Tether’s stablecoin reserves. In late November and early December 2024, representatives of Cantor and Tether, also representing Bitfinex, had ordinary course meetings to discuss various topics, including their existing relationship, where they also engaged in discussions regarding the formation and operation of a public company that would include holding and acquiring Bitcoin as part of its business operations, including the contribution by each of Tether and Bitfinex of 10,000 Bitcoin to such a business. Cantor advised Tether that it would explore the various ways to bring such a company public and present a proposed structure to Tether." [-Proxy Statement for Extraordinary General Meeting of Shareholders of Cantor Equity Partners, Inc. and Prospectus for up to 315,116,673 shares of Class A common stock of Twenty One Capital, Inc.](https://www.cstproxy.com/cantorequitypartners/2025/proxy/images/Cantor_Equity_Partners_Inc-EGMProxy2025.pdf)

19.214   In 2021, Tether "secured an account with Cantor Fitzgerald, and started converting its commercial paper assets to U.S. Treasury bills. Cantor had existing ties to Tether through its sister firm, BGC Partners, a trading desk that had bought and sold large volumes of Tether, according to a source with knowledge of the relationship." [-Forbes](https://archive.is/KU9ap)

19.2141   "Tether and Cantor had established a relationship in 2021 when Cantor began acting as a custodian and trading partner for a portion of the U.S. treasuries backing." [-Twenty One Capital, Inc. Draft Registration Statement on Form S-4](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2070457/000000000025008030/filename1.pdf)

19.2142   "Tether has additionally been using New York financial services giant Cantor Fitzgerald as a custodian of U.S. Treasury bills, three sources said." [--Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/sites/davidjeans/2023/02/10/tether-reserves-cantor-capital-union-ansbacher/)

19.2143   "Cantor Fitzgerald has been a Tether custodian since late 2021, Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino told The Block." [--The Block](https://www.theblock.co/news/markets/2024-01-16-cantor-fitzgerald-ceo-tether-reserves-272893)

19.2144   "Cantor custodies "the vast vast majority" of Tether's reserves, a person with direct knowledge of the matter told The Block." [--The Block](https://www.theblock.co/news/markets/2024-01-16-cantor-fitzgerald-ceo-tether-reserves-272893)

19.22   "Devasini has credited \[Richard] Heathcote with playing a key part in establishing the relationship with Cantor, a person with knowledge of the matter said. Heathcote acknowledged helping to connect the two firms while at Marlin Capital, adding that Lutnick was personally involved in the grueling due diligence process. Cantor started managing Tether’s reserves in 2021, media reports have said." [-Bloomberg](https://businessmirror.com.ph/2025/05/13/tethers-150b-cio-proved-himself-getting-cantor-backing/)

19.221   "Heathcote helped build Tether’s giant T-bill operation into an entity almost on autopilot: Buy bills with on average below 90 days duration at auction, hold until maturity, then repeat. 'It’s really not rocket science,' he said." [-Bloomberg](https://businessmirror.com.ph/2025/05/13/tethers-150b-cio-proved-himself-getting-cantor-backing/)

19.222   "Heathcote also played a key role nurturing Tether’s increasingly close relationship with Cantor Fitzgerald LP." [-Bloomberg](https://businessmirror.com.ph/2025/05/13/tethers-150b-cio-proved-himself-getting-cantor-backing/)

19.223   "HEATHCOTE, a graduate of Newcastle University, joined Tether as CIO in January 2023, succeeding Silvano di Stefano. He first met Tether Chief Executive Officer Paolo Ardoino and Chairman Giancarlo Devasini around 2018 while working as head of trading at Bahamas-based Deltec Bank & Trust, one of Tether’s banks." [-Bloomberg](https://businessmirror.com.ph/2025/05/13/tethers-150b-cio-proved-himself-getting-cantor-backing/)

items.title: There is No Such Thing as Price Gouging: Airline Shutdown Edition
items.text:
![](https://m.stacker.news/166604)

![](https://m.stacker.news/166605)

I saw a lot of economically ignorant tweets surrounding the recent shutdown of all flights nationwide by the FAA, so it's good time to re-iterate: there is no such thing as price gouging.

The rise in price of Ubers, hotel rooms, or supplies during any kind emergency is simply the product of demand rapidly rising, while supply remains fixed in the short term. Anyone who has seen a supply & demand graph can understand this phenomenon.

![](https://m.stacker.news/166611)

Moreover, it is good for victims of a disaster if you allow prices to rise.

Let's say a hurricane hits town, and the price of a gallon jug of water goes from $1 to $10. People from other towns will see an opportunity, and bring supplies from their town to sell for profit. But if you ban it under the guise of "price gouging," you're killing the incentive to do so, and, ironically, depriving the affected people of needed supplies. You're also creating a perverse incentive for whomever gets the store first to buy up a larger supply of water than they personally need, just because it's so cheap.

items.title: Bitcoin Arena: decentralized game & prediction market platform live on testnet4
items.text:
Hi there,

We built Bitcoin Arena: games and prediction markets on Bitcoin. It is fully decentralized. There is no company running the rounds, no central server and no custodian. Anyone can run a node, and anyone can offer an app. It’s live on testnet4, and we need people outside the team to try both.

There’s no token and nothing to buy. Test sats are free and have no value.

Anyone can run a node

* Install it on Windows, macOS or Linux. A setup window walks you through it.
* Post a bond on Bitcoin and take a seat.
* Host apps, verify rounds and earn a share of the fees.
* No permission needed. Your bond is your ticket in.

Anyone can offer an app

* Write your game and sign it, and any node can host it.
* The nodes replay every round with your rules.
* There’s no approval and no listing fee.
* You earn 2% of every paid round in your app.

How a round stays honest

* A Bitcoin block hash draws the committee of nodes, so nobody picks who decides.
* Stakes lock in a Fedimint federation run by the nodes.
* A result counts only when 5 of 7 nodes confirm the same one, and anyone can object for 10 minutes.

How you can help

* Run a node on testnet4 and tell us where setup was hard.
* Build a small app and tell us what’s missing in the docs.
* Play Tick Tock Next Block, Rock Paper Scissors or the 15-minute Bitcoin Up or Down market and try to break it.

items.title: Review of David Berri's Sports Economics, Chapter 1
items.text:
I started reading David Berri's textbook on Sports Economics in preparation for my upcoming [course](https://stacker.news/items/1586317), which has been approved by one committee and only needs approval by another before it gets the go-ahead.  I figured it would be helpful to both myself, and fun for stackers, to review each chapter as I go along.

## Chapter 1: It's Just Supply and Demand

Chapter 1 covers basic supply and demand theory that you would encounter in any introductory econ course, but he motivates it using sports examples, such as ticket prices, trading card prices, and player salaries.

I especially liked how he walked us through an analysis of a statement made by Obama, to show us why it's wrong.  Here's Obama's statement:

> "The biggest change I'd \[make right now as commissioner] is to figure out how to price tickets so that ordinary people can go to the games.  I mean, I think that ticket prices have gotten so high, and I understand that if salaries are high, ticket prices are going to be high, but you know, you hate to think that the only person that can go to a game is somebody who's got a corporate account."

Berri uses supply and demand to walk us through why, given that the supply of NBA tickets is pretty stable year-to-year because of a fixed schedule and fixed stadium capacities, the only explanation for rising ticket prices is growing demand.  Thus, rising ticket prices can't be caused by high player salaries; instead, it's more likely that both ticket prices and player salaries are high because of growing demand for the sport.

Along the way, he covers some other topics that are common to introductory econ courses:

* The effect of price controls, using salary caps as an example
* The difference between positive and normative statements, using "why do they get paid so much to bounce a ball" as an example
* The difference between deductive and inductive reasoning (no example given, but he said the rest of the book will be framed around that organization;  I think another way to say that is theory and empirics)

## What is this, a book for jocks?

The only thing I didn't like about the chapter was the problems at the end of the chapter.  I was expecting some problems that ask the student to use supply and demand creatively, like forecasting the price change in response to a new stadium buildout, for example.  Instead, the problems at the end are basically questions whose answers are given directly in the text of the chapter.  In other words, they felt like memorization questions.  And they were super simple too.  I'll be honest, I couldn't help but think that this book was written for dummies.  *Maybe it was written for jocks??*

In any case, I think smarter questions would have behooved the book well.  Maybe they're just simple because it's the introductory chapter.  We'll see if the problems get smarter as we go along.

## A problem for the stackers

But anyway, since the problems were too simple, I decided to make one up myself.  Let's see if stackers can handle some basic intro econ questions, as applied to the sports industry:

1. The MLB is considering the imposition of a salary cap.  Use supply and demand to illustrate how player salaries are determined currently, without a salary cap, then use the same diagram to illustrate what might happen to player salaries after the salary cap.  Use the diagram to discuss how player salaries might be affected immediately depending on the level of the new salary cap.  Explain how the salary cap might change players' decision-making during free agency (how will they choose which team to play for if all teams can only offer them the same salary?)

items.title: Are You Having Fun Staying Poor, Stackers?
items.text:
*Alternative title: **how do you tell the difference between a blip/dip and a final and complete collapse?***

This is *not* (primarily) a reflection on bitcoin's price debacle or the unwinding of the AI bubble or anything else going on in financial markets. The themes are, of course, overlapping and not unrelated/coincidental... but what *I'm getting at is life choices and professional "investments"/bets* and how to consider your situation etc (https://stacker.news/items/1617542).

...let’s start with our friend Jason Hodlers (@geekigai) and his call for help yesterday. It both disturbs me and generates a ton of empathy… “awfully relatable,” I wrote to a friend as I shared it, but also feeling really iffy it... (words like "reckless", "justice", "unfair", and "audacious" coming to mind.)

https://x.com/geekigai/status/2123313407927435724

Not in that *I am* in his situation, or have a dislocated shoulder, or have a family to support but that **you sacrifice the professional path you were on to do something you deeply believed in**. That’s admirable: we all want it, we certainly all want it to *work out,* and we celebrate those who do.... and those of us who do it (https://stacker.news/items/1513929) in *this* industry tell you over and over that you shouldn’t, it’s not all it’s made out to be, and actually *doing literally anything else* might be both financially better and professionally more secure.

Still, here we are and for some of us it goes *terribly* wrong.

You always gotta make a choice and a gamble: what industry to go for, what to study/learn, what career path, and in what country? **What are you good at, and what can you offer the world?**

## But what happens if what you have to offer isn't valued by others, or suddenly outcompeted by some technical advancement you didn't (couldn't) foresee?

AI has been hot and flourishing for years, and you were probably a geeky loser if you were into LLMs in the 2010s; bitcoin has been briefly hot now and again, but most of the time you're just a loser, having wasted your life and life savings on some stupid little internet experiment.

Jason describes how he and his wife — who is homeschooling some number of kids (because “god told us to” -- LOL. @. Dat) and has no ties to the labor market — two years ago decided that he should step down from his (fiat?) work and “focus all my time on building a local Bitcoin circular economy through @bitcoinchatt”.

Sure, we know how these things pan out — they don’t! — so that might have been reckless. But if/when this thing actually was a once-in-a-species monetary revolution, then this sort of local support/educational group would have been invaluable, picks-and-shovels style. And kudos to him for trying to build something real (and not financialized... not looking at anything or anyone in particular https://stacker.news/items/1617030)

…and when money got tight, he cleaned Airbnbs. Then fell and injured himself, so then he did even crappier jobs (on commission) that didn’t pay much… and then the thing he had built more or less fell apart.

Not able to buy groceries, he is “turning to the Bitcoin plebs for help”

> I have so little money right now (100% in bitcoin, except for some pocket change), I've hardly even felt this dip.

***

As @benmuse has been showing us — and the twitterati cope cheerleaders won’t shut up about — calm DCA **over long periods** has been pretty great in bitcoin (https://stacker.news/items/1616043). Problem: most of that benefit (not unlike the progress convo I’m having off-Bitcoin (https://stacker.news/items/1608876, https://stacker.news/items/1616353 ) came *years ago*. “Getting into bitcoin” this year or last has proved disastrous.

https://x.com/Bitcoin_phan/status/2123546470976766236

Yes, during the 2022 low-point we could *at least* blame the crazy frauds and paper bitcoin (https://stacker.news/items/1617378) and rates getting off zero, but in 2024-26 *everything* was set for this thing to work. If, at any point in bitcoin’s history, you wanted to sketch out the conditions under which we win, it would have *these* elements (ETFs, recognition, political turning point, regulatory clarity, *all these incredible services* etc etc) of the last few years.

Alas, it’s been among the worst-performing asset *something-something* around — flat for half-a-decade, unremarkable in anything but its hype-bubble-and-subsequent collapse. Don't look at the chart this week.

“Institutions,” as a [magic incantation](https://x.com/joakimbook/status/2123798010174099756), hasn’t generated net new buyers (https://stacker.news/items/1506425), either.

Everything is already built, we have *all the tools*, we *desperately* need a better/freer/safer/fairer money etc… **yet, it’s crickets over here. Nobody wants this, nobody likes this.** The most successful thing to come out of Bitcoin is Tether, a literal freedom dollar to arbitrage government interest expenses and the third world's poor access to dollars. https://stacker.news/items/1453638

(also, a TOTAL “Guy in corner of party” meme situation: or, more Stoically and Big-Shorty: "[I guess when someone's wrong, they never… they never know how."](https://www.magicalquote.com/moviequotes/i-guess-when-someones-wrong-they-never/))

I devoted my professional life to writing/editing, two tasks that machines now do, not necessarily “better,” but good enough and *especially* fast enough and cheap enough, that it’s mostly a work of charity/patronage at this point https://stacker.news/items/1610192. (Also, in the age of [AI and infinite generation,](https://stacker.news/items/1449095) nobody cares about human-written/-created content — at least not enough to pay for it — so rents, “value-add,” are mostly entirely competed away.)

## At what point should I (or Jason) have known better?

I dunno. I legit can't point to a moment at which he (or I) should have made better/different choices.

And it's the story of every (failed) start-up or business: You sacrifice/take a chance to pursue what you believe in and what you thought was important — only to find that it doesn't work out, and then bad shit happens, and then you’re screwed. (Doesn't help that, in the meantime, the asset you devoted your life to stops working and collapses in value before your eyes...) At any point in your start-up's journey, **you gotta gauge the trajectory and if this recent dip is a low point that will pass, or the turning point for total collapse.**

You can't know that, and the extremely lucky/rich AI peeps (https://stacker.news/items/1617039, https://stacker.news/items/1617406, https://stacker.news/items/1617680) are the flip side of that process. *Every corpse on Everest was once an extremely motivated/convicted person*...

I’m coming to this from a similar angle, my regret or bad-fork-in-the-road happening 12-14 years ago ([https://stacker.news/items/879698?commentId=879742](https://stacker.news/items/879698?commentId=879742)) in going to university; maybe 8-9 years ago in not getting a bullshit-fiat job after university; maybe 6 years ago moving to the end of the world; maybe 5-ish [years](https://bitcoinmagazine.com/markets/asset-bubbles-covid-19-make-bitcoin-case) ago, pivoting my work so much into the Bitcoin world https://stacker.news/items/1078866

At what point should I have known better? Is this a mere blip, a lull before a wonderful rebound, *or* critically, the beginning of the total end?

Obviously, you can’t know that and so you make the best of the skills/knowledge/hunches you have… Mises’ human action, *we’re all speculators, all the time* etc. https://stacker.news/items/1556891

Somehow Jason raised over [4 million sats](https://mempool.space/address/bc1q3k2mfct7mersgh9mkz3f8nc7y336pe62nc009m) from his ask, the value of which, unfortunately, is melting away like that proverbial ice cube. So I guess the takeaway is: *quit what you’re doing and live off someone else’s charity*. @Solomonsatoshi was right ALL ALONG. Incredible.

***

Finally, fate and efficient markets have a sense of humor: I told y'alls I've been trying **Invity**, this new, hyped,  European fintech/stacking company. https://stacker.news/items/1586158 https://stacker.news/items/1604577. Setting aside the fees and the hidden spread, they *do* give you €50/purchase bonus with a DCA program.

So the other day I caught this *perfectly* iconic and ironic screenshot for how **there are no free lunches** and this little orange dream of ours is, uh, a neat little dream designed for capital destruction. Saylor (and Bailey!) know a thing or two about that. 

![](https://m.stacker.news/167530)

*I was* gonna end this with a snarky little Den remark to just zap me scudos instead... but gold's exchange rate is collapsing *alongside bitcoin's* in a horrible reverse-debasement trade, so I guess **we all just stay poor instead.**

I dunno, man. Maybe McDonald's is hiring.

items.title: Why isn't bitcoin used for more gray market things?
items.text:
@spiral published The Long Road to Bitcoin Payments https://stacker.news/items/1603307/r/Scoresby last week and got quite a good discussion going here and on [Github](https://github.com/spiralxyz/bitcoin-payments/discussions/1).

Today, they are out with a summary of the community's response.

> **1. Global entrepreneurs, human or agent, earning in bitcoin.**
> **2. Agentic payments.**
> **3. Self-custody as stablecoins get more regulated and freezable.**

The guys on PBJ also did a recap of the discussion on their most recent episode, which is an interesting listen:

https://x.com/PresidioPod/status/2118070779959017814

There were two things that caught my attention in this conversation. First, @moneyball makes the point that it is surprising that the gray-market areas haven't seemed to find much use for bitcoin. 

# Why haven't the porn sites, online gambling dens, and illegal markets shown much interest in bitcoin payments?

While moneyball doesn't mention it, he made me think of Starbackr https://stacker.news/items/135689 https://stacker.news/items/67590 and after a little poking around it looks like they had some trouble with the App Store allowing zaps https://stacker.news/items/219407 but eventually managed a workaround https://stacker.news/items/224893 but then pivoted to AI https://stacker.news/items/250739 and quietly shut down -- at least the main starbackr website is no longer reachable (wayback machine last crawled it in [July 2024](https://web.archive.org/web/20240727123411/https://starbackr.com/) and shows a redirect to getcurrent.io -- last crawled by the wayback machine in Dec 2024 -- although you can still reach the [starbackr docs page](https://docs.starbackr.com/)). These guys seem to have made as good a run as any at delivering a bitcoin powered OnlyFans. What happened?

It seems that the same is true for online gambling (although maybe this story about [Iranian gambling sites](https://www.reuters.com/investigations/illicit-iranian-gambling-network-helped-pull-off-4-billion-sanctions-dodge-2026-07-31/) is a hint that bitcoin is being used in this manner? possibly we are all just too goody-goody to get invited to the illegal tables?).

I don't believe that traceability is the answer. As far as I can tell, porn sites and online gambling are mostly using credit card payments and tradfi banking, which is even worse for privacy. 

Spiral says that a lot of responses pointed out that there isn't any demand for bitcoin. But that seems to be answering the question with the question itself -- why isn't there any demand? 

# Surely someone needs money that no one can stop you from sending or receiving?

items.title: Financialization Everywhere: Starbucks and SN style (TDE, Jeff Degner)
items.text:
We've talked about this a lot: https://stacker.news/items/1598123, https://stacker.news/items/743123 https://stacker.news/items/869415

## Under a broken monetary system, EVERY COMPANY becomes money-printing banks

Airlines? *Banks*.
Card companies? *Banks*.
Universities? *Banks*
Hotels? *Baaaaanks*
Fintech firm Revolut? TOTALLY a *bank*.

...the latter is literally a bank, which issues fiat-denominated loans etc (https://stacker.news/items/1578425) but *also* prints points that conveniently plug into *other* shitcoin companies (airlines, hotels etc). 

**The ultra-financialization of everything...**

> In January 2002, shortly after the launch of the Starbucks Card, Michael Casey was its CFO and he reportedly gave a novel description of how Starbucks would use those funds. According to Allen Eslekin, the original Starbucks Card [program manager](https://peakportfolio.com/starbuckscard/), Casey was elated: **the program represented “a $20 million interest free loan from our customers”** that would reduce their reliance on banks for loans and operating cash.

Yeah, that's not how the customers think of them... but that's *entirely* what they are.

> In 2019, AIER contributor [J.P. Koning](https://aier.org/people/j-p-koning/) reiterated this illustration in his [*Moneyness*](https://www.moneyness.ca/2019/08/starbucks-monetary-superpower.html) blog. There, he explained that balances on gift cards amounted to $1.6 billion and “simultaneously function as a loan to Starbucks,” and customers are “providing the company with free debt.”

Love that. While JP's stance on Bitcoin has been between disappointing and retarded, he is/was spot on for this. One of the few online articles that have, in one fell swoop, altered my perspective.

![](https://m.stacker.news/165540)

## Are Cowboy Credits Shitcoins?

I mean, of course they are. 

SAME THING. They're interest-free finances for k00b et al. You can *call them* prepaid balances all you want, but if capital has a cost (Lightning channels, operational costs etc), then anything SN doesn't need to keep/hold one-for-one are freebies. *Duh*. (Fine, they're bitcoin-denominated liabilites, so that's less great if/when bitcoin appreciates, but if it doesn't?!)

...That they decay "fast" or can always be turned into SN-relevant services (posts, zaps, comments) is immaterial. Same goes for Starbucks:

> Lenders of money expect dollars back. Not so with a Starbucks gift card. The terms for a gift card purchase make it clear that the balance is “nonrefundable” and that it “may not be redeemed for cash,” unless required by law. What is owed is coffee or other Starbucks merchandise of the holder’s choice at an uncertain location sometime in the future.

## "According to their Q3 2026 SEC filing, Starbucks holds over $1.8 billion in “stored value card liability and current portion of deferred revenue.”"

> The economy of gift cards must also grapple with another reality: lost and forgotten cards. “Breakage” is the accounting term for those cards that are lost in the back of your kitchen junk drawer or that slid between your bucket seats.

My friend running partnerships for a certain old-school/fiat shitcoin (=loyalty) program confirms this... Breakage is *sort of* the point. The BEST possible money for them. \_I wonder what the "Breakage" equivalent is for Stacker and CC. If k00b et al were to produce income statements and balance sheet for their business (which, presumably, they do to investors/annual report style), **where would outstanding and non-used CCs sit?!**

> What breakage can’t do is produce cash. What it can do is to goose the earnings reports that shareholders and banks use to assess investment and lending decisions. In [FY 2025](https://investor.starbucks.com/news/financial-releases/news-details/2025/Starbucks-Reports-Q4-and-Full-Fiscal-Year-2025-Results/default.aspx), Starbucks’ operating cash flow fell by 22 percent compared to the [previous year](https://investor.starbucks.com/news/financial-releases/news-details/2025/Starbucks-Reports-Q4-and-Full-Fiscal-Year-2025-Results/default.aspx).

This isn't quite true. The cash was *given to Starbucks up front*! So the booking of breakage doesn't produce cash, sure, the company *had the cash all along*. That's what an interest-free loan MEANS.

> In this inflationary environment, holding a Starbucks gift card subjects one to an inflation tax. Prepaid cards experience a loss of purchasing power in the same way that holding cash balances do. Two years ago, that $25 gift card may have purchased five drinks at $5, but now may only get you four at $6.25 each.

We have a similar situation going on with CCs and bitcoin, since bitcoin's exchange rate travels/trades structurally *downward*. A CC created (and unused, unredeemed) at almost any point in the last two years is worth *less than it was when it was created*. Consumer missing out.

items.title: Microsoft is a Financial Engineer: Cash Flow Questions (FT, Kim & Armstrong)
items.text:
**Back to stock analysis basics!** [https://stacker.news/items/85150\&#x36](https://stacker.news/items/85150&#x36);**,** https://stacker.news/items/836811

*How's Microsoft doing?!*

![](https://m.stacker.news/164439)

## IT's All Just Financial Engineering?!

*Always has been*, idiot. https://stacker.news/items/1604239, https://stacker.news/items/1598123

> Last week, we wrote about how investors in the hyperscalers — Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle — are suddenly taking the decline in the companies’ free cash flow very seriously. (As, naturally, are the rating agencies — S\&P Global cut the outlook on Meta to negative just the other day, citing “significant uncertainty around capex and free operating cash flow”.)
> Microsoft stands out — it appears that, unlike its peers, it is not spending most or all of its cash profits that operations bring in. Correspondingly, Microsoft is the only one of the bunch with positive stock market returns over the last, bruising month:

![](https://m.stacker.news/164440)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164441)

and we care about this *why?*

> Investors like to look at free cash flow because metrics like operating profit and net income capture investment spending only through a smoothed measure (depreciation) and **do not capture swings in working capital items** (such as inventory, receivables and payables) that can dramatically affect a company’s economic position. Hyperscaler investors are, understandably, focused almost exclusively on the investment just at present.

* **GOOD** free cash flow is "fundamental profitability of the business." Selling stuff, you know, the good ole' fashioned reason to be in commerce. (LOL, say the diluting treasury companies... you can just scam your shareholders! https://stacker.news/items/1292636)
* **BAD** free cash flow is about financing (don't mention it to Saylor): terms, timing, BNPL on a corporate level, basically. 

> For example, a business might be able to pay its suppliers very slowly, while extracting instant payment from customers, which creates a growing stream of cash so long as sales are expanding.

## "This sort of financial engineering is not cheating and the company is admirably transparent about it."

> It is a source of real cash that can pay bills, be invested or simply collect interest. Indeed, there is a whole class of businesses that do nothing but co-ordinate various pools of capital with different financing arrangements. **They are called banks.** But free cash flow from financial engineering is often more volatile, less sustainable and harder to scale than cash that flows from profitable non-finance operations.

lol *sick buuuuurn!*

> Dave Zion of Zion Research Group [thinks](https://www.zionresearchgroup.com/blog/microsoft-s-free-cash-flow-would-be-negative-if-not-for-financial-engineering/) that *all* of Microsoft’s free cash flow comes from financial engineering. He thinks this engineering takes four main forms:

![](https://m.stacker.news/164442)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164443)

> The total of these and a few smaller adjustments is $75.3bn last year — more than 100 per cent of the company’s free cash flow. This does not mean that Microsoft is somehow hoodwinking investors. Powerful companies can extract good financial terms from suppliers, customers and investors and these terms have real value.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164444)

*Financial engineer? YES, I AM!* https://stacker.news/items/1514881?commentId=1514971

TL;DR, if you wanna fake (some portion) of your success, you can just print shares. In Saylor's case, it's to pay for expenses and interest to other shareholders (=Ponzi structure); for Microsoft it's to pay for employee compensation and capex.

items.title: If you're running LND, you may be vulnerable to a Linux kernel exploit
items.text:
Easiest thing to do is just shutdown LND for now if you aren't sure. I just did that myself (it's 7am here...)

This is *not* LND's fault. But golang sockets support the mptcp protocol by default, and unpatched linux kernels can be remotely exploited via mptcp via [CVE-2026-98432](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2026-98432). So if this command returns anything:

```
ss -Mlnp
```

...you are potentially vulnerable.

The fix is upgrading to a kernel that you know is not exploitable and restarting. Or even easier, just disabling mptcp. Heck, do both:

```
echo 'net.mptcp.enabled=0' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-disable-mptcp.conf && sudo sysctl -p /etc/sysctl.d/99-disable-mptcp.conf && sudo ss -Mlnp
```

items.title: BOOK on BOOKS: "Resistance Money", by Warmke-Bailey-Rettler
items.text:
Been slacking on my B\&A posts (but then again, it's *insanely competitive* over here; all the other assmilkers showed up to steal Den's rewards, so what's the point?? https://stacker.news/items/1614595), but I saw some *Resistance Money* posting yesterday and it reminded me that I *hadn't* actually released that on SN.

(Though somebody shared my article at TDE *way back*: https://stacker.news/items/573878)

Crazy.

***

[*Resistance Money: A Philosophical Case for Bitcoin*](https://link.amazon/B034tmzS1) was a cool, novel, interesting book that I used to recommend to people back then... at least *then*, bitcoin was interesting, optimistic, growing, and [flourishing](https://stacker.news/items/1616353). (Now, on the other hand, it's just dead, destroying itself, empty of cypherpunks and *astonishingly* financialized... gief **scodus**, please; no sats zaps)

![](https://m.stacker.news/167325)

*This review ran in Bitcoin Magazine Print's "Privacy Issue," the mentioning it of it here was a condition for me republishing the Book's Books review columns.*

***

## "Have no fear, the philosophers are here… and they say bitcoin is for criminals!"

> Yes, that *is* the message in this brand-new book by philosophy professors Andrew Bailey of Yale-NUS, Bradley Rettler of the University of Wyoming, and Craig Warmke of Northern Illinois University.
> But they also point out that bitcoin is for the downtrodden, for the dissidents in Russia or Venezuela or Ukraine, for Roya Mahboob and Alexei Navalny, for the poor without access to banking services, and anybody else living under a regime that wouldn’t allow them payments or property. By extension, posit the authors, it’s money for anyone who could ever imagine themselves being in a position where using resistance money is necessary for their very survival.

> For bitcoin to work as that tail-risk type insurance against authoritarianism, you need to acquire some and learn how to use it *before* that fateful event happens; **by the time the gatekeepers seal the exits, it’s too late to investigate escape hatches.** *You can’t take out insurance on the house when the flames already engulf the kitchen.* 

> Realizing that bitcoin works as money *precisely* *because* it works for all these people — the good as well as the bad, the criminal and money launderer as well as the freedom fighter and human rights activist — is the reason bitcoin is resistance money: Nobody can stop it. It’s the “most inclusive monetary network in the world” (page 269), a monetary network that nobody controls.

...Well, unfortunately the insurance premiums on this *increasingly stupid* insurance come in VAST, VAST capital destruction and negative returns. *Have fun staying poor*; and Den, please keep your intransigent editorializing away from uniquely written beautiful articles from the past...

> *Resistance Money* isn’t a technical book, though its explanation of bitcoin’s mechanics is thorough and excellent. But the authors still tell a comprehensive tale, with the dense and academic writing forcing the reader to always pay attention. The trio’s main argument is subtle: Is a world *with* bitcoin preferable to a world without it? If you could wave it away, should you? To *Bitcoin Magazine* readers that seems obvious enough, but the authors have a larger crowd in mind — speaking to the critics and doubters, taking care to seriously address the many-headed objections levied against bitcoin. They don’t overplay their hand, with plenty of hedging and nuance, no doubt as a result of publishing with a well-established academic publisher. They treat their subject matter with the utmost and careful intellectual rigor:

> > “Despite the hopes of many bitcoin diehards, it won’t end war, restore the traditional family, or fix the real estate market. It won’t improve nutrition, inspire a return to Renaissance-style art, or revive nineteenth-century architecture. Bitcoin does not fix everything. It fixes a few things—and even breaks some others” (page 14). 

> The unique angle that the authors bring to the table is a common philosophical device: **the veil of ignorance**. We shouldn't make moral judgments about systems or outcomes already knowing our place in that world, well aware of our capabilities and interests and wealth. We should decide what's a morally good world *not knowing* *who we will be in that world*. We shouldn’t answer questions about bitcoin’s merits and drawbacks, or prefer the incumbent fiat system over this uppity challenger “as the people we actually are; doing so would invite undue bias” (page 271).

> An investigative device commonly associated with John Rawls, the veil is a philosophical way of trying to assess outcomes more equitably:

> > “One by one, you live as every person in the world. You come to understand their dreams, joys, and struggles. You learn what’s important to them, how they flourish, and what impedes their flourishing. You learn important lessons about life in different circumstances. In the fullness of time, you forget your original self. One of those eight billion lives is your original life, but you can’t say which. The experiences meld together in a stew, none more or less important than any other” (page 74).

> The authors spend a lot of time, pages, and philosophical effort convincing us that even behind the veil we should indeed let bitcoin exist, but that judgment seems to fall remarkably short as well as almost trivially favor bitcoin by design. If there's a 1 in \~4 chance I will grow up unbanked or under an authoritarian government or censorious banking system, it almost doesn’t matter what potential benefits an infinitely printable fiat currency confers on the billion-or-so well-off in the West. Any benefit from a large welfare state or extra social security from a government with exorbitant monetary privilege is completely dwarfed by the ability of billions of people under authoritarian rulers to financially escape their much more dire situations. And I’m more likely to become them than I am benefiting from money printing. (I suppose that *is* the authors’ point.)

> By concluding that “we do think that behind the veil, you’d want to have this option available” (page 267), the authors sell themselves short. The philosophical case for bitcoin could do with a much more aggressive framing. It’s not even that cognitively demanding to say that a world *with* bitcoin is better than a world without it. Its mere existence, rather than its hyperbitcoinized success, helps some people infinitely but harms almost nobody. Put differently, even the most heartless critic is forced to confess that, yes, bitcoin is good for some select fringe cases. 

> A world where bitcoin fully wins is a world with pain. For it to succeed, a *lot* of people have to lose well-being, status, wealth, and employment. That loss will hurt on every human level — spiritually, emotionally, and materially.

> A strongly grounded philosophical case for why that pain is worth it, why the benefits of the incumbent system are dwarfed by the freedom, liberty, and human flourishing unleashed by bitcoin — now *that* would be a philosophical case worthy of these gentlemen’s attention. 

## "I hope they write a more ambitious follow-up."

**Selected quotes**:

* “Bitcoin does not merely institute an alternative monetary policy; it is a new kind of monetary institution” (page 107)
* “\[M]oney is helpful in living our best lives. In greasing the wheels of mutually beneficial exchange, it promotes human flourishing” (page 178)
* “Cash is indeed useful for all sorts of nefarious deeds. By offering financial privacy, cash has significant social drawbacks. And it’s worth it. \[…] Bitcoin and cash are of a piece in both of these respects. When it comes to privacy, what is true of cash is also true of bitcoin—they’re worth the trouble” (page 136)
* “Digital dollars can’t resist authoritarians; bitcoin does. Bitcoin is resistance money, and resistance money makes the world better. All things that make the world better come at a price, and bitcoin is no exception. But it is worth that price” (page 206)
* “No matter what happens to bitcoin, Satoshi’s discoveries will remain. We now know how to make digital cash, what it’s good for, and its tradeoffs” (page 275)

***
